passages.text: A multimodal transformer-based visual question answering method integrating local and global information

Addressing the limitations in current visual question answering (VQA) models face limitations in multimodal feature fusion capabilities and often lack adequate consideration of local information, this study proposes a multimodal Transformer VQA network based on local and global information integration (LGMTNet). LGMTNet employs attention on local features within the context of global features, enabling it to capture both broad and detailed image information simultaneously, constructing a deep encoder-decoder module that directs image feature attention based on the question context, thereby enhancing visual-language feature fusion. A multimodal representation module is then designed to focus on essential question terms, reducing linguistic noise and extracting multimodal features. Finally, a feature aggregation module concatenates multimodal and question features to deepen question comprehension. Experimental results demonstrate that LGMTNet effectively focuses on local image features, integrates multimodal knowledge, and enhances feature fusion capabilities.
1. Introduction

The rapid development of multimodal visual-language tasks has attracted extensive attention within the Computer Vision (CV) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) communities, leading to notable advancements and emerging research areas in related task. Visual question answering (VQA) poses huge challenge, as the model cannot identify the specific query content until it is input into the network, and different queries require diverse visual content; consequently, each object in an image varies in importance depending on the question.

Attention mechanisms have shown remarkable progress across deep neural network tasks, particularly within single-modality domains. In VQA, utilizing attention on the question to capture main terms is crucial for improving answer prediction. Recent studies indicate that involving both visual and linguistic information within the network can facilitate a common representation, achieving finer-grained semantic expression and thus enhancing model performance and prediction accuracy. However, these joint attention models have primarily captured only shallow interactions, with shared attention features lacking the complexity to support VQA model reasoning for intricate image interactions (e.g., object-question word relationships), thereby constraining model performance. To address this, researchers have proposed two joint attention models, which experimental results show are beneficial for understanding image-question relationships and enhancing VQA prediction accuracy. Notably, these models can be deeply cascaded, forming layered joint attention frameworks that support complex CV reasoning tasks, potentially boosting VQA effectiveness. Building on this, encoder-decoder structures based on attention have been designed to improve VQA model performance. Despite advances in VQA models, existing approaches primarily focus on global feature interactions, resulting in erroneous predictions for queries that require only localized information.

Multimodal fusion of visual-language features represents the most direct approach to solving VQA queries. This involves first extracting global features of the image as well as from the question, then predicting the answer based on a multimodal fusion model that maximally integrates both types of information. Several methods have introduced increasingly sophisticated models for feature fusion, utilizing advanced question feature extractors, multimodal fusion models with residual connections, bilinear pooling, and guided attention mechanisms. However, these approaches often apply question features to enhance visual attention, potentially over-emphasizing image features and overlooking the semantic essence of the question itself.

In summary, although recent methods have contributed to VQA model improvement, two main issues remain: (1) Current VQA models lack consideration for essential local image details during feature encoding, hindering accurate predictions for related queries; and (2) limitations in multimodal feature fusion impede fine-grained question comprehension, resulting in incorrect answer predictions.

To address these challenges, this study proposes a global-local attention (GLA) unit to emphasize prominent local visual features and integrates a self-attention (SA) module to model dense relations, such as word-to-word associations. A guided-attention (GA) unit is introduced to capture intensive cross-modal interactions between visual and linguistic features. Together, these three units form a foundational co-attention layer (CAL), with a deep vision-language encoding and decoding framework (D-VLEDF) constructed from stacked CAL layers. Additionally, multiple fusion strategies are applied during encoding and decoding to enhance question semantic comprehension, allowing the model to "see" relevant image features by using the query, and "hear" the query context in the multimodal representation module. The proposed network structure integrates these approaches to complete the VQA task effectively.
2. Related works
2.1 Methods based on multimodal feature fusion

VQA is a multimodal task requiring an understanding of both visual and linguistic knowledge. This involves mapping visual and linguistic features into a shared semantic space that captures the richness of multimodal knowledge. In early fusion methods, element-wise operations, such as multiplication, addition, or concatenation, are commonly used to combine visual and text features. Ren et al. are the first to use concatenation to fuse visual and question features, aiming to learn a joint representation. They represented all question words through summation. Shih et al. introduced an attention mechanism to select image regions relevant to the text query and map these visual and text features to a shared space, comparing their relevance through inner products. Similarly, Lu et al. emphasized that focusing on both visual and textual attention is essential and proposed a joint attention model to reason over image and question attention to achieve a multimodal fusion representation. However, these methods have limited multimodal feature representation capabilities, constraining the model's performance by restricting the amount of beneficial knowledge that can be derived.

To better model visual and linguistic features, researchers have proposed various fusion techniques. Kim et al. and Li et al. used element-wise multiplication for multimodal visual-language representation. Fukui et al. suggested that the outer product of visual and text features is more expressive; however, its high dimensionality makes it impractical. Therefore, they proposed a two-stage compact bilinear pooling method that first computes attention for images and questions for joint representation, then integrates it with the question representation for efficient fusion. While effective, this approach is primarily suited for high-dimensional features. Kim et al. addressed this limitation by using multimodal low-rank bilinear pooling with Hadamard products to reduce model parameters, although performance is sensitive to changes in hyperparameters. Building on this, Benyounes et al. proposed a multimodal tensor Tucker decomposition, designing a low-rank matrix decomposition method to explicitly constrain the interaction rank between visual and text representations. Yu et al. tackled the high-dimensional feature issue by integrating compact multimodal bilinear pooling and a joint attention mechanism, combines a "co-attention" mechanism with generalized high-order pooling for more discriminative image-question feature representation, improving multimodal fusion efficiency. Li et al. employed contrastive loss with cross-modal attention alignment before fusion, enhancing visual-language feature fusion. Dou et al. further improved VQA performance by inserting cross-modal attention within the visual and text encoding backbones.
2.2 Methods based on attention mechanism

Given their alignment with human cognition and interpretability, attention mechanisms quickly gained traction in VQA to advance research in this field. Yang et al. proposed the stacked attention network (SAN), which incrementally searches for question-relevant image regions based on question semantics, enhancing accuracy by associating visual information with questions. Anderson et al. used faster region-based convolutional neural network (R-CNN) to extract multiple object regions from images, then applied a bottom-up, top-down attention mechanism to identify relevant image regions, capturing essential visual features. Schwartz et al. introduced a general attention mechanism to learn high-order associations among data patterns. Recognizing that visual elements are often isolated in conventional attention mechanisms, Patro et al. introduced attention weights based on different support and opposition samples, making attention more akin to human perception and aiding answer prediction. Nam et al. proposed dual attention networks (DANs) to link specific image regions and question words through multiple steps, allowing visual and text attention to guide each other for collaborative reasoning, particularly effective in VQA. Peng et al. proposed an attention framework that enhances connections between query keywords and image areas by simultaneously mapping relevant object regions and identifying associated words. These methods improve representation learning for both visual and textual modalities to better predict answers. Moreover, Nguyen et al. proposed a simple yet symmetric architecture for visual and language representations, facilitating iterative interactions between image-question pairs. Gao et al. introduced a dynamic approach to integrate intra- and inter-modal information flow, capturing higher-order interactions between questions and image regions to enhance VQA performance. Yu et al. presented a multi-level, cascaded co-attention network to model intra- and inter-modal relationships. Guo et al. calculated similarity between visual regions and question words, refocusing on image objects aligned with answers, reconstructing initial attention maps for consistent results. Tian et al. developed a sequential top-down attention model to highlight essential details derived from both images and questions, suppressing irrelevant details, allowing more granular interactions for full multimodal fusion.
2.3 Reasoning-based visual question answering methods

Current VQA models typically focus on feature extraction without enhancing reasoning capabilities. In response, recent studies have developed reasoning mechanisms for processing extracted visual and linguistic features. Andreas et al. proposed a neural modular network with modular layers ("Find, Transform, Combine, Describe, and Measure") to predict answers, dynamically instantiating module networks based on question language substructures. Although effective, this method requires a natural language parse tree to generate substructures. Hu et al. addressed this by proposing an end-to-end modular network that adjusts network structure and learns parameters without requiring pre-defined language substructures. Chen et al. introduced a meta-modular network that dynamically configures function modules for complex visual reasoning. Akular et al. developed language-guided adaptive convolutional layers, allowing the model to co-attend to salient features within visual and textual information.

Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have gained traction in VQA because of their effectiveness in capturing both global and local relationships. Teney et al. used GNNs to represent relationships among scene objects and question words, inspiring Brown et al. to propose a graph-based VQA approach incorporating a graph learner module that captures image representations specific to the question. Hu et al. proposed a language-conditioned graph network to capture relationships among objects and between objects and language. Khademi et al. introduced a multimodal neural graph memory network for VQA. Hudson et al. enhanced model interpretability by incorporating a neural state machine that predicts a semantic relation probability graph for the image, performing sequential reasoning on the probability graph to evaluate effectiveness.
2.4 Existing issues with current methods

VQA requires simultaneous understanding of visual and textual content, with the fusion of these multimodal features for effective answer generation. Efficient VQA model performance relies on accurate text and image feature extraction and effective multimodal feature fusion. However, current VQA methods face several challenges: (1) Existing VQA models often only capture global visual features, neglecting crucial local details, which are often necessary for accurate question answering. (2) Insufficient interaction between visual and textual modalities. Although attention mechanisms are employed, they generally prioritize image regions guided by questions, lacking reciprocal guidance of text by image. Additionally, interference control between features during fusion remains underexplored. (3) Most VQA approaches operate as classification tasks (selecting the correct answer from a set of options), which falls short in real-world applications where generative answers are more applicable. Moreover, there is no standard evaluation mechanism for generated answers. (4) Limited model interpretability. Current VQA methods do not explain the reasoning behind answer selection. An interpretable network design is needed to provide justifications alongside answer predictions.
3. The proposed LGMTNet

To overcome the shortcomings of the Transformer's self-attention mechanism in distilling local details and insufficient multimodal feature fusion, a GLA and dual fusion strategy for visual-language features are proposed. This approach emphasizes key local features within global image representations while enhancing multimodal integration, thereby improving model performance. The proposed method is structured into three main components: an advanced vision-language encoding and decoding framework and decoding module, a multimodal feature representation learning module, and a question-feature and multimodal feature aggregation module. The structure of LGMTNet is presented in Fig 1. The visual feature extraction module employs ResNet-101 to extract image features, with an input size of 224 x 224 and an output feature map of dimension  . Global average pooling is then applied to obtain the final visual feature representation . The textual feature extraction module utilizes a gated recurrent unit (GRU) to process the input text sequence, with an embedding dimension of 300 and a hidden state size of 512, resulting in a final text feature dimension of . Therefore, an additional GA unit is incorporated in the multimodal representation module (MMR), reinforcing the understanding of "what to hear" and further strengthening the visual-language feature integration. 3.2.1 High and low frequency attention mechanism.

Essentially, the low-frequency attention branch (Lo-Fi) is designed to capture broad feature dependencies, leveraging global attention without requiring high-resolution feature maps. Conversely, the high-frequency attention branch (Hi-Fi) captures detailed local dependencies, which necessitates high-resolution feature maps and operates effectively with local attention. Each of these attention types is discussed in detail below.

Hi-Fi primarily encodes fine-grained local details. Applying global attention to the feature map could inadvertently connect unrelated objects, hindering model optimization. Hence, Hi-Fi is designed to capture detailed features within local windows, thereby reducing computational complexity. Unlike time-intensive operations such as window-shifting or multi-scale window partitioning, Hi-Fi utilizes a non-overlapping window partitioning approach, which is more hardware-friendly.

Recent studies have demonstrated that global attention in MHAtt can effectively capture low-frequency information. However, directly applying MHAtt to high-resolution feature maps incurs substantial computational costs. In low-frequency attention (Lo-Fi), average pooling:acting as a low-pass filter:is first applied across each channel to extract low-frequency signals from the input features. These pooled feature maps are then mapped into keys  and values , with s representing the window size. Queries Q in Lo-Fi are derived from the original feature map, allowing standard attention to capture comprehensive low-frequency information across the feature map. With reduced spatial dimensions for keys K and values V, Lo-Fi significantly lowers the computational complexity of MHAtt.

The initial allocation of heads in Hi-Fi and Lo-Fi follows the original number used in MHAtt. However, excessive head counts may increase computational costs. To optimize efficiency, the heads from MHAtt are split into two groups with a defined ratio ;  heads are allocated to Hi-Fi, while the remaining  heads are assigned to Lo-Fi. This split reduces the computational load of HiLo, as both attention mechanisms are less complex than standard MHAtt. An additional benefit of this head-splitting strategy is the reduction of model parameters by decomposing the learnable parameter matrix  in Eq. (12) into two smaller matrices. 4. Experiments and conclusion analysis
4.1 Experimental datasets and evaluation metrics
4.1.1 Dataset.

VQA has been a research focus for several years, resulting in the development of numerous datasets. These datasets have grown significantly in size and contain increasingly comprehensive annotations. The commonly used datasets in VQA research include COCO-QA, VQA-1.0, VQA-2.0, and Visual Genome. The experiments are designed with the VQA-2.0 dataset.

The VQA-2.0 dataset is an extension of the VQA-1.0-real dataset, specifically designed to mitigate language biases inherent in VQA-1.0-real. By addressing these biases, VQA-2.0 prevents models from relying on language priors to achieve higher prediction accuracy, facilitating the development of more interpretable VQA models that focus on visual content. Specifically, the VQA-2.0 dataset includes 82,783 images with 443,757 questions for training, 40,504 images with 214,354 questions for validation, and 81,434 images with 447,793 questions for testing. This dataset is approximately double the size of VQA-1.0 and is divided into three categories: "Yes/No," "Number," and "Other." Additionally, each question corresponds to two visually similar yet distinct images, enabling the model to generate different answers. This dual correspondence effectively reduces bias and imbalance in the dataset.
4.1.2 Evaluation metrics.

VQA models are trained to automatically answer questions based on visual and linguistic information. Evaluation metrics primarily assess whether the predicted output matches the correct answer, with Accuracy as the primary metric.

Ren et al. framed VQA as a classification task, using Accuracy (Acc) as the standard performance metric for VQA models. However, in practical applications, a question may have multiple correct answers. To account for this, Antol et al. provided multiple human-annotated answers for each question. In this study, the experiments rely on the VQA-2.0 dataset, using Accuracy as the evaluation metric. Higher values indicate better model prediction accuracy. 4.2 Experimental environment and network parameters

Hardware requirements: This study is conducted on a server running Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS, with the following specifications: CPU - Intel  Xeon  E5-2650 V4 @ 2.20GHz x 48, RAM - 128GB, GPU - NVIDIA TITAN V with 12GB memory. To enhance training efficiency, two GPUs are utilized.

Software requirements: Python 3.7, PyTorch 1.7, and CUDA 11.7 are used. PyTorch, a Python-based scientific computing library, enables flexible model adjustments and optimizations through dynamic computational graphs. With built-in optimizers like SGD, Adam, and Adagrad, PyTorch facilitates the implementation of various optimization algorithms.

Experimental parameter settings: Image features are extracted using ResNext152, pre-trained on Visual Genome, yielding visual features with dimensions of 256 x 2048 after max-pooling, further mapped to 256 x 512 for computational convenience. For textual features, question lengths are set to 16, with 300-dimensional GLoVe embeddings processed through a GRU to obtain language features of 16 x 512 dimensions. The attention module employed 8 heads, each with a dimension of 64. During training, the batch size is 64, and the learning rate is updated per the function , where t represents the current epoch, starting from 1. After 10 epochs, the learning rate is reduced by a factor of 5 every two epochs. Adam served as the optimizer, with the model trained for 13 epochs in total.
4.3 Comparison with other methods

BAN employs a bilinear attention network to extract bilinear interactions between image regions and question words, generating joint representations through low-rank bilinear pooling. DFAF alternates intra- and inter-modality interactions across visual and linguistic modalities, improving predictive performance. ReGAT uses graph attention to model interactions among multiple object types within each image, learning adaptive relations for questions and target objects, thus improving prediction accuracy. MCAN captures self-modal and image-guided attention through deep co-attention modules, improving answer prediction accuracy. MMnasNet constructs a deep encoder-decoder backbone with a task head for VQA, enhancing answer accuracy. Re-Att refocuses visual information in images based on answer information, achieving strong performance. APN introduces an automatic parsing network that identifies and leverages latent tree structures in data, enhancing Transformer-based vision-language systems' efficacy in VQA and image captioning. ARAC proposes a fully attention-based VQA architecture, including an answer-checking module that applies unified attention to common answers, questions, and image representations, updating the answer. MCAoAN develops an attention module (AoA) to clarify relationships between attention maps and query sets, yielding a final feature matrix by multiplying an attention weight matrix with the attention map.

Table 1 shows that the proposed LGMTNet outperforms other algorithms on the VQA-2.0 test set, achieving overall accuracies of 72.04% and 72.29% across two test sets. Compared with MCAN, LGMTNet improves Test-dev accuracy by 1.41% and Test-std by 1.39%, showing respective gains of 1.28% and 2.07% in Number and Other question types. Significant improvements are also observed over ReGAT, with LGMTNet's overall accuracy surpassing it by 1.77% and 1.71% on the two test sets. These findings confirm that the proposed global-local relationship attention mechanism enhances the model's focus on local salient features, supporting more accurate answer prediction and improving VQA performance.

5. Conclusion

This study introduces a multimodal fusion VQA network based on Transformer architecture, designed to improve the representation of local visual features and comprehension of semantically integrated features. The model combines global-local attention, multimodal representation, and feature aggregation modules and employs three foundational attention units to construct a deep encoder-decoder, enhancing visual-language fusion for enriched semantic understanding. The multimodal representation module enables the network to focus on key query words, and image-guided question attention mitigates linguistic noise in the VQA task. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed model's effectiveness in capturing fine-grained visual and language features, offering a novel approach to VQA model performance enhancement.

Future work, given the continuing advancement of AI and CV, will address (1) more effective multimodal fusion methods, (2) improved model interpretability, and (3) further optimizations for existing VQA algorithms.

passages.text: Potential biomarker and composite efficacy readout for human clinical trials of schistosomiasis vaccine in Africa

Schistosomiasis is a chronic disease that inflicts high morbidity and significant mortality with an estimated 90% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. Development of a vaccine against schistosomiasis is a major global health goal. The SchistoShield (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE) vaccine has consistently exhibited robust efficacy in non-human primate pre-clinical trials, has recently completed Phase 1 clinical trials in the US and Phase 1b trials are ongoing in Africa. To delineate a potential clinical/parasitological endpoint to measure the efficacy of schistosomiasis vaccine during human clinical trials, we have designed an in vitro schistosomula killing assay using sera collected from SchistoShield-vaccinated baboons and human volunteers from the Phase 1 clinical trial. Sm-p80-specific antibodies produced by immunized non-human primates and humans induced statistically significant larval schistosomula killing ex vivo. This reproducible functional assay has the potential to serve as one of the biomarkers for the effectiveness of the SchistoShield vaccine in human trials in Africa.
Introduction

Parasitic diseases remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide and disproportionately affect people living in the poorest regions of the world. Significant progress has been made in reducing the burden of human infections through the Millennium Development Goals and the Sustainable Development Goals. However, we are constantly faced with new challenges resulting from changing environments, mainly by influencing the distribution of snail intermediate hosts, and age-related infection patterns within human population that increase the threat of schistosomiasis, a neglected tropical disease caused by dioecious flatworms of the genus Schistosoma. At least six geographically distinct species of Schistosoma, particularly S. mansoni, S. haematobium, and S. japonicum, are responsible for infections in humans that result in over 290,000 deaths per year. Currently, schistosomiasis is endemic in 78 countries with over 250 million people living with the disease and an estimated 800 million people at risk. The clinical manifestations of schistosomiasis are considerable and include fever, anemia, genital lesions, growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly and permanent organ damage resulting in an estimated 3.3 million disability-adjusted life years. In addition, the disease also inflicts a heavy socio-economic burden on affected communities.

Efforts to control schistosomiasis have included strategies ranging from disease treatment, to managing complications, controlling the spread of the disease through integrated approaches such as mass drug administration (MDA) with praziquantel (PZQ) and targeting the snail intermediate host and improving the sanitation. The ambitious targets set by the World Health Organization (WHO) for the global schistosomiasis control based on large-scale MDA using PZQ have not been met due to a multitude of logistical challenges - including shortfalls in drug delivery, patient adherence, sustained reinfection rates and inadequate infrastructure. Although mass PZQ administration - as advocated by the WHO - seems to be effective in the short term, it is unsustainable in the long term. PZQ controls morbidity in patients by killing established adult schistosomes, however - due to its ineffectiveness against juvenile worms and sustained reinfection rates - the overall effect on disease transmission is transient as prevalence return to baseline levels within a very short period of time. Further, the development of drug resistance by the parasite is also a concern that requires reevaluation. Additionally, interruptions in MDA programs often lead to the occurrence of severe rebound of the disease sequelae - particularly in high-transmission areas. Furthermore, disease transmission is now being reported in new locales that were previously schistosomiasis-free, perhaps due to global warming and the emergence of hybrid parasites. In light of these issues, the deployment of an effective vaccine in concert with current control measures represent a prudent and logical approach for achieving elimination.

Over the course of two decades, our group has developed a potent schistosomiasis vaccine, termed SchistoShield, targeting a functionally-important S. mansoni calpain protein. SchistoShield has been extensively tested in numerous animal models and has consistently exhibited protection at all intra-mammalian parasite life cycle stages. A Phase 1 safety, reactogenicity and dose-escalating clinical trial for SchistoShield (https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05292391) has recently been completed in the USA. In this trial, no safety concerns have been observed in all of the groups including with dose escalation. The vaccine was well tolerated and seroconversion of all of the vaccinated individuals with pronounced vaccine-mediated humoral responses was observed. Furthermore, we are currently evaluating the vaccine-mediated cellular immune response in all of the trial participants, which is one of the important effector arms for vaccine development. Phase 1b trials of SchistoShield in endemic region of Africa are currently ongoing in Madagascar and Burkina Faso.

The present study was designed to identify and further evaluate a potential clinical endpoint to measure the efficacy of the schistosomiasis vaccine during human clinical trials and beyond. In this study, we describe a reproducible functional assay in which the killing of larval schistosomula was measured using sera/antibodies obtained from baboons and humans vaccinated with SchistoShield. This biomarker has the potential to serve as an important constituent of the composite efficacy endpoint panel and may also be useful in dosing schedule optimization for future clinical trials in Africa.
Results
In vitro killing of S. mansoni schistosomula using pre-clinal trial sera samples from the baboon model

To examine SchistoShield vaccine induced antibody mediated killing of S. mansoni schistosomula in vitro, sera were collected from baboons that were immunized using a 2-dose and 4-dose vaccine strategy (Fig. 1a). Mechanically-transformed S. mansoni schistosomula were cultured in vitro in complete media containing SchistoShield-vaccinated baboon sera with or without exogenous complement. Sera obtained 8 weeks after the last immunization achieved 64.7% schistosomula killing efficiency (p = 0.0021) in the 2-dose group (week 16) and 54.3% (p = 0.0365) killing in the 4-dose vaccine group when compared to control sera. Killing efficiency was significantly amplified in the presence of exogenous complement (2-dose 75.1%, p = 0.0011; 4-dose 69.6%, p = 0.004) (Fig. 2a). A similar trend of schistosomula killing efficacy was observed with sera obtained at 26 weeks (before the cercarial challenge) and 34 weeks (euthanasia) after the last immunization. The killing efficacy of 2-dose and 4-dose immune sera was 62.6% (p = 0.0007) and 62.4% (p = 0.0001) with the addition of exogenous complement increasing the rate of killing slightly to 68.9% (p = 0.0013) and 68.9% (p = 0.004), respectively (Fig. 2b). At euthanasia (34 weeks post-vaccination), 53.4% (p = 0.0003) and 43.8% (p = 0.0004) schistosomula killing was observed in the presence of 2-dose and 4-dose immune sera, respectively. Moreover, the percentage of schistosomula killing increased when immune sera were supplemented with exogenous complement (Fig. 2c). Heat inactivation of both sera and complement resulted in baseline killing efficacy comparable to the control sera and media alone (Fig. 2a-c).

Schematic representation of the pre-clinal vaccine efficacy trials in baboons. Schedules of vaccinations with SchistoShield vaccine, S. mansoni cercariae challenge and blood collection are shown (Panel a). Panel (b) illustrates the vaccination schedule with SchistoShield for the phase 1 clinical trial in healthy humans and subsequent blood collection.

S. mansoni schistosomula killing with vaccinated baboon sera. Mechanically transformed schistosomula were incubated in complete media, either alone or supplemented with pooled sera, and with or without exogenous complement. The percentage killing of schistosomula at 8 weeks (Panel a), 26 weeks (Panel b), and 34 weeks (Panel c) post vaccination is shown. Percent parasite killing was determined by comparing the experimental groups to the control. 2D C and 2D E represent 2-dose control (GLA-SE) and experimental (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE), respectively, while 4D E represents the 4-dose experimental group (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE). Error bars denote average +- S.E. P values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. HI = heat-inactivated; Comp = exogenous complement.
In vitro killing of S. mansoni schistosomula using sera collected from subjects vaccinated with SchistoShield in human phase 1 trial

Sera were collected from healthy participants in the SchistoShield phase 1 trial. A three-dose vaccination strategy including a delayed booster was adopted for the trial (Fig. 1b). Incubation of S. mansoni schistosomula with pooled sera from human volunteers immunized with SchistoShield demonstrated a significant killing of the parasite (Fig. 3). The micrographs show the morphological changes in schistosomula including granulation, bleb formation, and membrane integrity loss, following incubation with sera obtained from the study groups of the volunteers in the presence of exogenous complement (Fig. 3).

In vitro schistosomula killing assay using sera (Day 181 for groups A, B, D, E, and Day 304 for group C) from the phase 1 clinical trial of SchistoShield. Panel (a) illustrates schistosomula in RPMI-1640 media alone. In contrast, morphological changes indicative of schistosomula killing were evident when incubated with pooled sera from vaccinated volunteers. Panel (b) depicts the killing observed using sera from Group A (100 microg Sm-p80), the unadjuvanted antigen-only group. Similarly, Panel (c) shows schistosomula killing with sera from Group B (10 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE), while Panels (d), (e), and (f) illustrate the results for Group C (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, delayed booster), Group D (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE), and Group E (100 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE), respectively. Arrows (panels b-f) show morphological changes especially blebbing and membrane disintegration.

The percentage killing of schistosomula mediated by sera from the human subjects immunized with different doses of vaccine is presented (Fig. 4): antigen alone [100 microg Sm-p80] (Fig. 4a), low-dose [10 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE] (Fig. 4b), mid-dose [30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE] (delayed booster) (Fig. 4c), mid-dose [30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE] (Fig. 4d), and high dose [100 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE] (Fig. 4e). There was a significant increase in schistosomula killing trends across all vaccinated groups at all time points compared to normal human sera collected pre-vaccination (day-0) (Fig. 4a-e). In all vaccinated groups, the highest percentage killing of schistosomula was observed when heat inactivated sera were supplemented with exogenous complement, whereas the lowest percentage of schistosomula killing occurred when sera were heat inactivated. Except for day 57 in group C, where the highest schistosomula killing (71%) occurred on day 57, the killing percentage across the other vaccinated groups (A, B, D, and E) was observed on day 181 (124 days after the second boost), reaching approximately 74%, 72%, 70%, and 70%, respectively. On day 85, the second highest percentage of schistosomula killing was observed in the preparations where sera were supplemented with exogenous complement. On day 85, we observed around 59%, 65%, 46%, 46% killing in Group A, B, C, E respectively, whereas in Group D around 55% killing was observed on day 57. Furthermore, we also observed schistosomula killing with sera alone preparations, which was around 48%, 37%, and 39% on day 57 in Group A, B, and C respectively. However, in the sera alone preparation the maximal killing was observed on day 181 for group D (42%) and E (38%). Across all the groups, the lowest percentage of schistosomula killing was noted with heat inactivated sera (Fig. 4). Interestingly, across all groups on day 8 after the first vaccination, we observed a notable increase in schistosomula killing compared to day 0. This shift in killing may be due to IgM mediated complement fixation.

Sera from the Phase 1 clinical trial of SchistoShield (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE) demonstrated efficient killing of S. mansoni schistosomula in vitro. Schistosomula killing was observed with sera collected from phase I trial Group A (100 microg Sm-p80 alone, Panel a), Group B (10 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Panel b), Group C (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE/delayed booster, panel c), Group D (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, panel d), and Group E (100 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, panel e). Across all groups, the highest percentage of schistosomula killing occurred when heat-inactivated sera were supplemented with exogenous complement. In contrast, heat-inactivated sera alone consistently showed the lowest killing efficacy in all study groups. Day zero indicates pre-vaccination normal human sera collected before any vaccinations. Error bars denote mean +- S.E.M. The differences in schistosomula killing were statistically significant at the 95% confidence level with p < 0.05 (between p = 0.04 and p < 0.0001) on Day 181 (Groups A, B, D, and E) and Day 304 (Group C) across all preparations, except in Group B (when serum samples were compared with heat-inactivated sera), and when serum samples were compared with sera plus exogeneous complement preparations for Groups A, B, D, and E (p > 0.05). Similarly, the results were statistically significant with p < 0.05 (between p = 0.04 and p < 0.0001) when day-0 (pre-vaccination) sera were compared to post-vaccination day 181 (Groups A, B, D, E) or day 304 (for Group C) sera, except for Group B and Group C, when pre-immunization serum samples were compared with Day 181 and 304 serum samples (p > 0.05), respectively. V = Day of vaccination.

In addition to the pooled sera, we randomly selected three individual serum samples from each of the five groups to assess schistosomula killing in the in vitro assays. We selected individual sera samples from groups A, B, D, and E collected on day 0, day 57 (four-weeks after the second immunization), and day 85 (four-weeks after the third immunization). Whereas for group C (delayed booster), we selected sera samples collected on day 0, day 8, and day 208. We observed efficient killing of S. mansoni schistosomula in vitro across all groups (Fig. 5). Analogous to pooled sera, individual serum samples demonstrated the highest killing percentage of schistosomula when heat inactivated sera was supplemented with exogenous complement. Whereas heat-inactivated sera resulted in the lowest killing percentage across all individual volunteers tested.

Sera collected from volunteers in the phase 1 clinical trial using SchistoShield (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE) showed efficient killing of S. mansoni schistosomula in vitro. Schistosomula killing was observed with sera collected from three randomly selected volunteers across all five groups; namely sera from Group A (100 microg Sm-p80 alone, Panel a), with sera from Group B (10 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Panel b), with sera from Group C (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE/delayed booster, Panel c), with sera from Group D (30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Panel d), and with sera from subjects enrolled in Group E (100 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Panel e). The highest percentage of schistosomula killing was observed when heat-inactivated sera were combined with exogenous sera added to schistosomula in selected volunteer's sera from all study groups; whereas heat-inactivated sera showed the lowest killing efficacy in all volunteers across the study groups. Day zero refers to pre-vaccination normal human sera from the vaccinated volunteers. Day-57 sera were collected before the third immunization (four weeks after the second immunization), and Day 85 sera were collected (in Groups A, B, D, and E) or Day 208 (in Group C) four weeks after the third immunization. Error bars represent mean +- S.D. The differences in schistosomula killing were statistically significant at 95% confidence level with p < 0.05 (between p = 0.04 and p < 0.0001) at Day-85 (Groups A, B, D, and E) and at Day 208 (Group C), except for when serum samples were compared with heat-inactivated preparation in serum samples CTMID-1079 (Group A), CTMID-1564 (Group B) and CTMID-1290 (Group E) (p > 0.05).
Discussion

The life cycle of digenetic schistosome parasite encompasses complex asexual and sexual phases including the necessity of requiring an intermediate snail host. This multicellular helminth parasite, Schistosoma mansoni resides in the hepatic portal system. The   and   worms live in pairs - the   worm resides inside a gynecophoric canal of the   parasite (in copula), with an average longevity of 3-10 years for this association. A single   can produce up to 300 eggs/day and the entrapment of these eggs in different organs (liver, spleen and intestine) causes granulomatous reactions and fibrosis which are the principal clinical manifestation of chronic disease. To survive in an immune hostile environment, hemo-helminth schistosomes utilize surface membrane biogenesis and turnover, as a means to dodge host immune responses. The Sm-p80 antigen (the antigenic component of SchistoShield vaccine) plays an important role in the immune escape by the parasite and is also implicated in additional immune evasion tactics, including cleavage of host CD23, as well as degradation of fibronectin to inhibit blood clot formation around the worm in vivo. Due to the absence of a vaccine against any of the helminth parasites including schistosomes, the determination of vaccine effectiveness will undoubtedly involve a number of immunological (protective cellular and molecular responses) and parasitological readouts and biomarkers.

To determine SchistoShield vaccine efficacy, reduction in worm burden (prophylactic efficacy), decrease in egg retention in organs (pathology-resolving efficacy) and egg excretion in feces combined with the diminishing ability for eggs to hatch (parasite transmission blocking efficacy) are important parameters that will require quantitative assessment. Therefore, a multidimensional composite efficacy group of biomarkers and readouts will be required to assess vaccine efficacy. In our continual efforts to improve and refine this process, we have recently measured inhibition of enzymatic activity mediated by Sm-p80 antibodies from animals and human using a soluble recombinant variant of Sm-p80 that retains catalytic activity and is termed B7. This functional inhibition assay is one of the potential vaccine surrogates of protection and can serve as an important component of a larger composite efficacy readout panel which will encompass the components of antibody-/T-cell-mediated effector functions and estimation of circulating anodic antigen (CAA). As a logical extension, in this study, we have further developed a potential endpoint based on the ex vivo killing of schistosome larvae. Using mechanically transformed schistosomula, important data on vaccine-mediated protection in animal models of infection and disease has been reported. Similarly, an in vitro killing assay has also been used to screen potential drug targets against schistosomiasis. As reported previouslyin this study robust killing of schistosomula via sera collected from baboons vaccinated with SchistoShield was observed. We have observed significant killing with vaccinated sera even without exogenous complement (Fig. 2, D E week 16) compared to the corresponding control sera (Fig. 2 C week 16, panel a). The results become more evident when we compared killing at week 24 (2D E week 34, panel b). We observed an increase in killing with exogenous complement, especially with human sera; however, the increases were moderate indicating that exogenous complement by itself had a minor impact on killing schistosomula. Sera collected from SchistoShield phase 1 trial human subjects were equally potent in killing schistosome larvae in all of the different dosing groups. The baboon study vaccination protocol used in this study was designed to simulate harsh conditions of endemic areas to determine the vaccine efficacy using clinical endpoint and immunological readouts that will be used in human efficacy trials. Important to note is that at least up to 4-6 months, following the last vaccination, both baboon and human sera were effective in killing the larvae which highlights the longevity of Sm-p80-specific antibodies. Based on these data, it appears that antibody responses associated with this parasitological endpoint both in baboons and humans. For phase 2 clinical trials, biomarkers (e.g., B7-inhibition assay and in vitro killing of schistosomula) combined with IgG titers, and CAA levels could be important in making gating decisions, however, an important factor to note is that the higher level of variability is often observed with functional/biological assays. These two endpoints that are well-characterized have the potential to serve as important surrogates of correlates of protective immunity and vaccine efficacy. Finally, studies are currently being planned to decipher the mechanism of SchistoShield action on different life cycle stages of the parasite, effect on growth of the parasite and immune evasion by the parasite.
Methods
Non-human primates, parasites and ethics statement

Papio Anubis (olive baboons), aged 2.15-2.81 years, were acquired by the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center (OUHSC) and housed in their Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International-accredited facilities. The animal studies were approved by the OUHSC Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol number: 18-013) and Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center-IACUC (protocol number: 20010202). All of the procedures were followed were in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. The study was conducted as per ARRIVE standards.

Biomphalaria glabrata snails infected with Schistosoma mansoni (Puerto Rico PR-1 strain) were procured from the NIH/NIAID Schistosomiasis Resource Center, Biomedical Research Institute (Rockville, MD).
Pre-clinical trial samples: immunization strategy and Sera collection from baboons

A total of 16 baboons were randomly divided into three groups: control (n = 3), experimental group 1 (n = 7) and experimental group 2 (n = 6). Each baboon in the experimental groups was immunized with 250 microg Sm-p80 formulated in 50 microg GLA-SE (Sm-p80 + GLA-SE, SchistoShield) while each of those in the control group received 50 microg GLA-SE only intramuscularly. Baboons in experimental group 1 received a primary immunization at week 0, followed by a single boost at week 8 (2 doses), while the animals belonging to experimental group 2 received a primary immunization at week 0 followed by three boosts at 4-week intervals (4 doses). Immunization regimen for the control group is the same as that of experimental group 2. Twenty-six weeks (6 months) following the last immunization, each baboon was percutaneously challenged with 1000 S. mansoni cercariae. Eight weeks post-challenge, baboons were euthanized to determine different parameters of vaccine efficacy. Baboons were euthanized according to the American Veterinary Medical Association Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals 2020 Edition (https://www.avma.org/sites/default/files/2020-01/2020-Euthanasia-Final-1-17-20.pdf) using exsanguination under a surgical plane of anaesthesia followed by administration of concentrated sodium pentobarbital. During the course of this experiment, sera samples were collected as outlined in Fig. 1a.
Human clinical trial samples: vaccination schedule of Sm-p80 + GLA-SE (SchistoShield) vaccine

A phase 1, randomized, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of the Sm-p80 + GLA-SE (SchistoShield) vaccine in healthy adults was conducted at the Kaiser Permanente Washington Health Research Institute, Seattle, WA, USA (Registration date: 23/03/2022, ClinicalTrials.gov ID, NCT05292391) using approved protocol (DMID 18-0018; IRB approval through Advarra Inc., Columbia, MD., USA). Prior to enrolment, informed consent was obtained from each trial participant. This human study was conducted in compliance with the International Council for Harmonization and Good Clinical Practice and other applicable guidelines and regulations. Briefly, this trial was composed of 5 treatment groups with nine human volunteers enrolled in each group. Prior to the vaccination at day 1 blood was collected from each subject. Group A (unadjuvanted comparator) received 100 microg Sm-p80 alone, Group B (low dose standard schedule) received 10 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Group C (mid dose delayed booster) received 30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, Group D (mid dose standard schedule) received 30 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE, and Group E (high dose standard schedule) received 100 microg Sm-p80 + 5 microg GLA-SE. Each volunteer in all the groups received primary immunization at day 1. Subjects in group A, B, D, and E received two booster doses 4 weeks later at day-29, and 4 weeks from the first boost at day-57. Subjects in Group C received first boost at day-29 and second boost at day-180. Blood samples were collected and sera isolated from trial subjects prior to each vaccination, on the day of vaccination, at 7 and 28 days after each vaccination, and at 124 days after the last vaccination. Samples from timepoints demonstrating Sm-p80-specific IgG antibodies were pooled and used for the in vitro killing of schistosomula. Vaccination strategies and blood collection schedules are summarized in Fig. 1.
Shedding of snails, cercarial transformation and in vitro killing of Schistosoma mansoni schistosomula
S. mansoni cercariae were shed from snails by exposure to light at 28  C for 1.5 h. Cercariae were transformed mechanically into schistosomula by repeated passes through a 22 gauge needle syringe.

In vitro schistosomula killing assays were performed using the sera collected from pre-clinical (baboon) and clinical human trial subjects. The following sample preparations were included in the study. Schistosomula in the presence of Sm-p80-immunized baboon or human sera (1:50 dilution) or heat-inactivated Sm-p80-immunized baboon or human sera (1:50 dilution) with or without exogenous complement sera from guinea pig (1:50 dilution) (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO). Sera were heat inactivated by incubating samples at 56  C for 30 min. The pre-treated schistosomula samples were cultured overnight at 37  C with 5% CO2 in complete RPMI-1640 media (RPMI 1640 (Cytiva-HyClone, Logan, UT) supplemented with 100 microg/mL penicillin G (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), 100 microg/mL streptomycin (Sigma Aldrich St. Louis, MO), 10 microg/mL gentamycin (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) and 10% fetal bovine serum (ThermoFisher Scientific, Greenville NC) with a density of approximately 50 schistosomula per well in 2 ml of media using a 24-well plate (Corning Costar).

Schistosomula were observed under bright field at 10-10x magnification with an inverted microscope (Nikon, Model TMS) to identify as live or dead based on morphological changes (presence of blebbing, granularity and/or membrane integrity loss) and motility. The number of dead and viable schistosomula were counted in each well. Percentage schistosomula killing was computed by dividing the number of dead schistosomula in each well by the total number of schistosomula in that well, then multiplying by 100. Likewise, percentage protection was calculated as follows: (% protection) = (% killing of schistosomula in Experiment - % killing of schistosomula in Control) / % killing of schistosomula in Experiment x 100. Schistosomula percentage killing average of the three wells was computed for each sample preparation. Efficiency of killing among the different sample preparation was assessed by the difference between the percentage of dead schistosomula in the presence of active and inactivated complement. Each assay was carried out with three technical replicates per sample preparation. Micrographs were captured using a camera (Leica, Model DMi1).
Statistical analysis

Data from in vitro schistosomula killing experiment were analyzed via GraphPad Prism 9. We applied paired student t-test to compare the statistical difference in schistosomula killing in each group comparing day 0 (pre-vaccination) versus post-vaccination day 181 for groups A, B, D, E, and for group C, day 304 (end of the study time point). In addition, comparisons were also made between different sera preparation used in vitro killing assays. P-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

passages.text: Glandless, a tomato HD-ZIP transcription factor, is important for the gland formation of type VI trichomes
SUMMARY

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a model plant to study glandular trichome development and their specialized metabolism, and several transcription factors (TF) regulating these intertwined traits and their network have been functionally characterized. Among them are members of the homeodomain leucine zipper subfamily IV (HD-ZIP IV). Here, we study a tomato EMS-mutant line, glandless, presenting mutant, glandless type VI trichomes with a consequential reduction in volatile terpene levels. This mutant trichome also has some morphological characteristics of a type IV trichome. The glandless mutant has altered trichome densities, and acylsugar biosynthesis is slightly increased. As verified via virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS), the gene underlying this phenotype is SlHDZ38, the first member of HD-ZIP subfamily I found to regulate the development and specialized metabolism of glandular trichomes. Additionally, we show that the expression of an intricate network of known trichome-related regulatory TFs and biosynthetic enzymes is affected by the glandless mutation. Overall, our results contribute to the elucidation of the network of TFs controlling tomato trichomes.
Significance Statement

We studied a tomato EMS-mutant plant, glandless, that has glandless type VI glandular trichome. The gene underlying this phenotype is a member of the HD-ZIP subfamily I, which regulates the development and specialized metabolism of type VI glandular trichomes.

How the formation of glands of glandular trichomes is regulated or controlled is not well understood. By selecting a tomato mutant with type VI trichomes without a gland and identifying the responsible Glandless gene, we now know a key player in this process.
INTRODUCTION

Among adaptations in vascular plants to interact with the environment, the hair-like structures called trichomes are found in approximately one-third of the species with vastly diversified morphologies (Fahn, ; Payne, ). Glandular trichomes and their metabolites are critical for plants to cope with abiotic and biotic stresses and to attract pollinators (Bickford, ; Tian et al.,; Wagner et al., ). Trichome metabolites have also been exploited as high-value ingredients in the food, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical industries, and as natural pesticides in agriculture (Schilmiller et al., ). Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) has become a model species to unravel the regulation of development and specialized metabolism of multicellular glandular trichomes in horticultural crops (Feng et al., ). In fact, cultivated tomato accessions and their wild relatives display different combinations and densities of eight types of trichomes, four nonglandular (type II, III, V and VIII) and four glandular (I, IV, VI, VII) (Glas et al., ; Luckwill, ). The latter are distinguished by their morphology, the number of cells, and the chemical classes of compounds found in them (McDowell et al., ). Type VI trichomes are composed of a basal cell, a long stalk cell, a small intermediate cell, and four glandular cells where mostly mono- and sesquiterpenes, but also flavonoids and methylketones, are produced (Akhtar et al., ; Bleeker et al., ; Fridman et al., ; Nakashima et al., ; Schilmiller et al., ). These metabolites are deposited in the intercellular cavity in the middle of them (Bergau et al., ; Tissier et al., ).

Recent research has started to unravel the complexity of glandular trichome development in tomato, but there is still much to be learned. Up to now, several tomato transcription factors (TF) have been characterized as regulators of type VI trichome development and metabolism. These mostly belong to the MYB (MYELOBLASTOSIS), bHLH (basic helix loop helix), ZFP (Zinc finger protein), GRAS (GAI, RGA, SCR) and HD-ZIP (homeodomain leucine zipper) transcription factor (TF) families. The latter, only present in plants, is characterized by a homeobox domain (HD) and a leucine zipper motif (ZIP) and comprises four classes (I-IV) that differ in functional domains (Gao et al., ; Zhang et al., ). To the subfamily IV belongs SlWO (WOOLLY), a master regulator of trichome type I, III, V, VI, and VII differentiation (Vendemiatti et al.,; Wu et al., ; Yang, Li, Zhang, Luo, et al., ; Yang, Li, Zhang, Wang, et al., ). It has been recently suggested that trichome fate during development is controlled by SlWO via a dose-dependent mechanism. The SlWO protein concentration is regulated by self-activation of its gene and via negative feedback regulation by SlMTR1 and SlMTR2 (MULTICELLULAR TRICHOME REPRESSOR), previously characterized as trichome regulators with the names SlCYCB2 and SlCYCB3 (Gao et al.,; Wu et al.,). Low levels of SlWO activate SlLFS (LEAFLESS), which promotes type VI and VII development, while high SlWO levels activate SlMX1 (MIXTA) and SlWOX3b (WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX). SlMX1 and SlWOX3b form a complex that promotes type I, III, and V development also by repressing SlLFS (Wu et al., ). SlWO interacts independently with several of the other characterized trichome regulators. An additional role for SlMTR1 in regulating SlWO at the post-transcriptional level has been suggested because of their protein-protein interaction (Wu et al., ; Yang, Li, Zhang, Luo, et al., ; Yang, Li, Zhang, Wang, et al., ). Specifically related to type VI glandular trichome development, it has been proposed that under the regulation of jasmonic acid (JA) via SlJAZ2 (JASMONATE ZIM-DOMAIN) and SlJAZ4, SlWO interacts with SlMYC1 (MYELOCYTOMATOSIS). The resulting SlWO-SlMYC1 complex binds the promoters of TPS (TERPENE SYNTHASE) genes and activates their expression in mature type VI trichome gland cells (Hua et al., ; Hua et al., ). Additionally, SlWO binds to two C2H2 zinc finger TFs known to regulate nonglandular trichomes, SlH (HAIR) and SlSH (SPARSE HAIR) (Chang et al., ; Chun et al., ; Hua et al., ; Li et al., ; Zheng et al., ). It has been suggested that in this three-way interaction, they cooperate in regulating the formation of multiple types of trichomes (Chang et al., ; Chun et al., ; Zheng et al., ). SlLN (LANATA) is another recently characterized HD-ZIP IV transcription factor, whose natural mutant shows a higher density of hairy trichomes (type I, III, and V) and lower density of type VI and VII glandular trichomes (Xie et al., ). SlLN interacts with SlH and binds to an L1-box in the SlH promoter, positively regulating its expression. Moreover, similar to SlWO, SlLN binds to the promoter of both SlMTR1 and SlMTR2, activating their expression. SlLN interacts with SlWO, enhancing transcriptional activation of SlMTR1 and SlMTR2 and promoting trichome formation (Xie et al., ). To the HD-ZIP subfamily IV belongs also SlCD2 (CUTIN DEFICIENT 2), a regulator of cuticle formation of epidermal cells that positively impacts type VI trichome density (Nadakuduti et al., ). Lastly, the HD-ZIP IV TF SlHD8 (HOMEODOMAIN PROTEIN 8) is involved in trichome types I, III, V, and VI initiation and morphogenesis. SlHD8 regulates SlHl (HAIRLESS) and its homolog SlHl-2, coding respectively for two interacting subunits of the WAVE (WASP-family verprolin-homologous protein) regulatory complex for actin filaments nucleation. SlHD8 function is required for the JA-induced trichome elongation by enhancing the expression of proteins determining the loosening of the cell wall and is regulated by SlJAZ4 (Hua et al., ; Kang et al., ; Kang et al., ; Xie et al., ).

passages.text: Although in the last decade many studies have led to the discovery of tomato genes involved in type VI glandular trichome development, a comprehensive regulatory model is far from being achieved. In this study, we characterized glandless, a tomato mutant where type VI trichomes miss the glandular head cells and do not accumulate volatile terpenes. Additionally, we identified the mutated gene coding for a novel HD-ZIP TF, named SlHDZ38, the first of subfamily I linked to trichome regulation in tomato. With virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) we further confirmed that SlHDZ38 is indispensable for the gland development of type VI trichomes. SlHDZ38 is also involved in controlling the densities of other trichome types. Altogether, these results provide new insights in the regulation of type VI glandular trichome development.
RESULTS
Phenotype of a new tomato trichome mutant

To select tomato plants with aberrant type VI trichomes, the trichomes of 8000 individuals from an EMS-mutagenized population were phenotyped with a stereo microscope. Previously, in another EMS population, the myc1 mutant had been identified (Xu et al., ). In this study, we identified a mutant with aberrant trichomes missing the glandular cells of type VI glandular trichomes, and for this reason, it was named glandless (Figure 1a,b). Visually, the most evident phenotype of glandless plants seemed a reduced density of hairy trichomes on leaves (Figure 1c,d), stems (Figure 1e,f) and sepals (Figure 1g,h).
Phenotype of glandless mutant.

Type VI glandular trichomes as seen with an EVOS inverted light microscope on leaves of RZ-2 wild-type (WT) (a) and on the glandless mutant (b) tomato. Comparison between wild-type (WT) and glandless leaves (c-d) and trichomes visible on respectively wild-type (WT) and glandless stems (e-f) and sepals (g-h).
The glandless mutant has aberrant type VI glandular trichomes

To fully investigate the trichome morphology on the glandless mutant plant, leaf (Figure 2a,b) and stem surfaces (Figure 2c,d) were imaged using Cryo-SEM. Architecture and dimensions of nonglandular hairy trichomes of type III and V were not different between RZ-2 wild-type (WT) and glandless on both leaf sides and on stems. Likewise, on glandless leaves, glandular trichomes of type VII and of the rarely occurring type I were like the WT. Instead, detailed inspection of type VI trichome morphology supported our previous observations as no trichomes resembling the WT type VI (Figure 2e) could be found on the stem and leaves of glandless (Figure 2f). The novel trichome type in this mutant emerges from a single simple epidermal basal cell similarly to type VI and has a comparable-sized stalk supporting, presumably, a single cell. However, the stalk is formed not by one but by two, or sometimes three, cells, suggesting a possible alteration in the cell division pattern. The four gland cells forming type VI trichome head are absent and, in their place, glandless type VI trichome heads exhibit a single rounded cell. Comparison with type IV trichomes on cotyledons (Figure S1) indicates similarities between the mutant type and type IV trichomes, which are normally absent from adult leaves (Glas et al., ; Vendemiatti et al., ). However, the top cells seem to be different from the single gland cell of type IV trichomes (Figure S1). In tomato, the metabolites in the glands of type IV and VI trichomes can be released when physically damaged by a stretched-out glass Pasteur pipette (Kortbeek et al., ; McDowell et al., ; Tissier et al., ). However, on glandless, the single round apical cell could not be ruptured in this manner, suggesting it to be an intermediate cell rather than a gland cell. Overall, these results suggest that a mutation in glandless involves a gene regulating type VI trichome development causing the observed anomalous morphology.
Morphology of glandless trichomes on leaves and stems.

Cryo-SEM images of RZ-2 wild-type (WT) leaves (a) and stems (c, e) and glandless mutant (MUT) leaves (b) and stems (d, f). Arrows indicate the different types of trichomes and the cell types that constitute type VI glandular trichomes.
Leaf trichome densities are different in glandless mutant

To examine whether the glandless mutation influences also trichome densities, Cryo-SEM images of both the adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces were examined. On both the adaxial (AD) and the abaxial (AB) leaf surfaces, no difference was observed in the number of type I and III trichomes, but significantly fewer type V trichomes were found on both leaf sides (Figure 3a,b; Figure S2). On the AD side, there were significantly more mutant type VI trichomes on glandless than normal VI trichomes in the RZ-2 WT but not on the AB side of the leaves (Figure 3a,b; Figure S2). Instead, type VII glandular trichomes had lower density on the AB but not on the AD side (Figure 3a,b; Figure S1). Overall, the trichome density is much reduced in the glandless mutant (Figure 3c) and the number of the different type of trichomes was also changed (Figure 3d). The number of the different types of trichomes on sepals also differed between the mutant and the WT (Figure S3). Altogether, these results indicate that the selected glandless line is a new trichome mutant that presents not only altered type VI trichome morphology but also has different type V and type VII densities.

In the glandless mutant the levels of volatile mono- and sesquiterpenes are reduced

To study whether the lack of the four glandular cells on the glandless mutant also impacted the production of volatile terpenoids synthetized and stored in type VI glandular trichomes, monoterpene (alpha-pinene, 2-carene, alpha-phellandrene, alpha-terpinene, D-limonene, beta-phellandrene trans-beta-ocimene, terpinolene, linalool), and sesquiterpene (beta-caryophyllene and alpha-humulene) levels were quantified on RZ-2 WT and glandless mutant (Figure 4 and Figure S4). In the glandless mutant, all the measured mono- and sesquiterpenes were significantly reduced on both stems (Figure 4a,b) and leaves (Figure 4c,d). Similar results were observed also when analyzing 200 gland cells manually isolated from type VI trichomes on leaves from the RZ-2 WT and the corresponding cell left on the new trichomes in glandless (Figure 4e,f). These results show that the glandless mutation affects the levels of volatile mono- and sesquiterpenes suggesting either that glandless directly regulates terpene biosynthesis or that the reduction is an indirect effect of the alteration of type VI glandular trichome morphology.

Glandless is mutated in Solyc09g008810

The glandless mutation was fine-mapped to chromosome 9, specifically to the Solyc09g008810 gene (Figure 5a; Data S1). To determine the mutation, the genomic sequence of this gene in the RZ-2 WT and in the glandless mutant were cloned and sequenced. The glandless allele presented a T to A substitution in position 938 near the 3' end of the first intron. This single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) introduces a premature acceptor splicing site (AG) that causes a 10 bp frameshift to the coding sequence (CDS) of the gene that results in an early stop codon after a stretch of seven amino acids (Figure 5a). To confirm that this mutation is responsible for the observed trichome phenotype, a functional analysis of the Solyc09g008810 gene was performed using VIGS in S. lycopersicum cv. Micro-Tom. We also targeted eGFP as a negative control and SlPDS1 (phytoene desaturase) as a visible control, as it leads to photobleaching. After 5 weeks, microscopical observations revealed that compared with the negative control, leaves in which Solyc09g008810 was targeted had patches with aberrant type VI glandular trichomes that resembled the morphology of the ones observed on the glandless mutant (Figure 5b). Accordingly, the levels of known mono- and sesquiterpenes were reduced (Figure 5c). Therefore, we concluded that the Solyc09g008810 gene, carrying the SNP site in the glandless mutant, is responsible for the mutant trichome phenotype observed on this line. Overall, these results demonstrate that a mutant allele of the Solyc09g008810 gene is responsible for the trichome phenotypes in the glandless tomato mutant, suggesting that the encoded protein controls the development of type VI glandular trichomes.

SlHDZ38 is a new candidate regulator of tomato trichomes

The Solyc09g008810 gene is predicted to code for a 241 amino acids long uncharacterized protein with a homeobox domain, widely reported to mediate specific binding to DNA, and a leucine zipper motif, that is known to mediate formation of protein dimers. This classifies the protein as part of subfamily I of the plant-specific HD-ZIP TF family. In tomato, a total of 49 genes belong to it (Hong et al., ) and Solyc09g008810 gene encodes SlHDZ38. To gain more insight in its functions, the amino acid sequence of SlHDZ38 was used to find homologs via BLASTp on the NCBI nonredundant protein database. The homology research returned many HD-ZIP-I TFs from various plant species, including hemp, grapevine, poplar, cotton, and cucumber (Figure 6a). The alignment of the selected plant homologs of SlHDZ38 revealed a high level of conservation among HD-ZIP I transcription factors, particularly in the regions of the homeobox domain (Q63-A122) and the leucine zipper motif (K123-L157) (Figure 6b). The closest homolog in Arabidopsis thaliana is ATHB51 (HOMEOBOX 51) also known as ATLMI1 (LATE MERISTEM IDENTITY 1). Remarkably, in Cucumis sativus, a TF characterized as a regulator of trichome differentiation was found, encoded by the CsGL1 (GLABROUS 1; Csa3G748220) gene, whose mutant alleles named CsGL1, CsMICT (MICRO-TRICHOME), and CsTBH (TINY BRANCHED HAIR) all show a glabrous phenotype (Q. Li et al., ; Pan et al., ; Zhang et al., ; Zhao et al.,). The glandless allele, due to an early stop codon, encodes for a 39 amino acid long protein that completely lacks both the DNA-binding and the dimerization domains (Figure 6c). These results corroborate our finding that the glandless phenotype is caused by the mutation in SlHDZ38.

SlHDZ38 glandless mutation alters the expression of trichome-specific regulatory and metabolic genes

With the aim to study the impact of the mutation at the transcriptional level, RNA sequencing was performed on leaves, including their trichomes, and isolated stem trichomes of RZ-2 WT and glandless plants (Table S2). The expression of genes already known to be involved in trichome development and in type VI trichome-specific metabolism was analyzed. In leaves, seven mono- and sesquiterpene synthase genes were less expressed (Table 1). Additionally, reduced expression was found for the JA signaling inhibitors SlJAZ2 and SlJAZ4 that control SlMYC1 and its interaction with SlWO, essential in the regulation of type VI trichome development and terpene metabolism (Hua et al., ; Xu et al., ). Slightly but significantly lower transcript levels in glandless leaves were also observed for SlMTR1 and two HD-ZIP TFs, SlLN, and SlHD8, all three involved in trichome development. SlGCR1, one of the two recently identified MYB-like TFs that inhibit the formation of trichome gland cells (Chang et al., ) was also found to have lower expression levels in glandless. These results support the double role for SlHDZ38 as being involved - directly or indirectly by modulating the levels of other TFs - in controlling volatile mono- and sesquiterpenes biosynthesis and regulating trichome development.

Many terpene synthases were among the lowest expressed genes also in isolated stem trichomes, including the type VI glandular trichome-specific SlTPS9 and SlTPS5 (Table 2). Dramatically reduced were also the transcriptional levels of SlEOT1, SlEOT2, SlMYC1, and SlSCL3, that share a particularly high expression in trichomes and function as transcriptional regulators of terpene biosynthetic pathway genes (Spyropoulou, ; Spyropoulou et al.,; Xu et al., ; Xu, 2023; Yang et al.,). In the isolated stem trichomes of glandless, among factors known to be involved in trichome development, SlSH, SlMIXTA-like and the HD-ZIP IV TFs SlHD8 and SlCD2 had higher transcript levels. Moreover, SlWO and two of its downstream targets in hairy trichome regulation, SlMX1, and SlWOX3b, were all upregulated. Accordingly, SlMTR1 a negative regulator of SlWO showed lower expression, while its homologs SlMTR2 and SlMTR3 had higher expression. Lastly, the JA signaling inhibitors SlJAZ5, SlJAZ6, and SlJAZ7 were also more expressed in glandless than in WT.
