passages.text: Whole hempseed as a feeding enrichment for laying hens: effects on egg quality, nutritional profile and sensory attributes

To evaluate the effect on egg quality of the dietary supplementation with whole hempseeds, as an environmental and nutritional enrichment, a 4-week trial was implemented in an aviary housing a total of 1800 Hy-Line Brown hens in 8 pens (225 hens/pen). From 37 to 40 weeks of age, four pens received only a commercial diet (Control group) and the remaining four pens received whole hemp seed (HS group) (10 % of the average daily feed intake of the whole group) once per day in two additional circular feeders (two pens) or directly on the ground (two pens). Then, for the specific purposes of the presents study, after 14 and 28 days of trial (60 eggs/pen per sampling), a total of 480 eggs were collected from two pens of the control group and the two pens of the HS group fed hemp seeds in the circular feeders. On average of the two samplings, the hempseed enrichment did not influence most egg quality traits, i.e. proximate and mineral composition of egg yolk (P > 0.05), while it reduced the L* index and the pH of yolk (P < 0.001) and increased the pH of albumen (P < 0.05). Additionally, in yolk, hempseed enrichment decreased the proportion of total saturated (P < 0.001) and monounsaturated fatty acids (P <= 0.05), whereas it increased the proportion of n-3 (P < 0.001) and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (P <= 0.05) compared to hens of the control group. Sensory evaluation of boiled eggs showed that 46 % of the participants noted the difference between eggs from hens receiving or not the hempseed supplementation (P <= 0.05), but one sample was not preferred over another (P > 0.05). In conclusion, the enrichment after four weeks with whole hempseeds at 10 % of the daily feed intake in laying hens improved the fatty acid composition of yolk lipids without affecting the majority of egg quality traits and consumers' preferences.
Introduction

In response to the rapid population growth, food industry is compelled to achieve maximum food production while prioritizing respect of animal welfare, food safety, and quality, driven by consumer demand-oriented approaches. In this framework, eggs play a significant role in food security, being the most affordable among animal proteins without any restrictions on cultural and religious grounds. As for the production system, consumers perceive eggs produced in systems other than cages as having added value in terms of ethics, acceptability, and taste. Additionally, consumers request healthy functional food to prevent nutrition-related diseases and improve physical and mental well-being, while the nutritional properties of food are the major factors in purchase decisions. In detail, consumers are largely interested in food enriched with n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), considering that dietary intake of n-3 PUFA, especially eicosapentaenoic (EPA) and docosahexaenoic (DHA) acids, has been linked to reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases. Nevertheless, consumers exhibit hesitancy in altering their dietary patterns, which implies the need to transform regularly consumed foods into functional foods by modifying their composition. In this direction, eggs have the potential for enrichment with various essential nutrients, including n-3 PUFA to serve as a functional food for human consumption. To this purpose, different sources of n-3 PUFA, including fish oil, flax, and microalgae, have been successfully incorporated into laying hen diets to increase the PUFA content in eggs.

The evaluation of candidate n-3 PUFA sources requires a comprehensive assessment, encompassing considerations for potential impacts on both egg quality traits and sensory attributes. Due to its rich nutritional composition, hemp seeds could be considered a suitable feed for animal feeding. The authorized hemp seed (Cannabis sativa) cultivation for specific varieties listed in regulation (EC) No. 2860/2000, wherein the main psychoactive compound, THC, is legally restricted to a maximum content of 0.2 % (w/w). In that sense, the inclusion of hemp in the diets of laying hens, as whole hemp seeds, cakes, and oil, has been found to increase PUFA deposition in yolk, without affecting egg sensory attributes nor transferring tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) or cannabinoid residues in eggs.

To the best of our knowledge, limited studies have evaluated the effects on egg quality of using hemp seeds over the diet normally fed to laying hens in a cage-free system as an environmental enrichment. In fact, this housing system is widely used to meet consumers' demand for more welfare-friendly eggs. In these systems, welfare concerns include feather pecking, skeletal injuries, and increased mortality and different types of enrichments, including feeding enrichments, may play a positive role in their mitigation by providing hens increased behavioral possibilities. Moreover, previous studies showed that n-3 PUFA supplemented diets can reduce bone breakage and increase bone strength in free range laying hens.

Based on available literature, a level of inclusion equal to 10 % of daily intake for feeding enrichment is the minimum to modify the egg quality (foraging and nutraceutical effect) and permit a suitable environmental enrichment to reduce aggressive behavior and feather peaking among hens. While suggested the maximum level of whole hemp seeds or hempseed cake should be 5 % to 7 % of the diets for laying hens, a recent meta-analysis by showed that these dietary inclusion levels are too low to modify the FA profile of the eggs.

Thus, the present study aimed to evaluate the effects of whole hemp seeds used as an enrichment in laying hens kept in a cage-free system on egg chemical, physical, and rheological properties, cholesterol and mineral content, fatty acid profile, and sensory traits.
Material and methods
Housing and management of laying hens and diets

This study was conducted in the facilities of the Experimental Farm "Lucio Toniolo" of the University of Padova, Italy. The experiment was approved by the Ethical Committee for Animal Experimentation (Organismo per la Protezione del Benessere Animale, OPBA) of the University of Padova (Project 28/2020, prot. 204398, approved on 06/05/2020). All animals were handled according to the principles stated by the EU Directive 2010/63/EU regarding the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. The researchers involved in animal handling were either animal specialists (PhD or MSc in Animal Sciences) and/or veterinary practitioners.

The experimental aviary (2.50 m wide x 19.52 m long x 2.83 m high) consisted of 3 tiers and a litter area on the ground. Two corridors were available for the hens adjacent to the two sides of the aviary, so the floor space was 6.01 m wide x 19.52 m long. The aviary was divided into 8 pens (2.50 m wide x 2.44 m long x 2.83 m high), each one hosting 225 animals at housing time (18 week of age) for a density of 9 hens/m2 of available area (including the tiers). Each pen was equipped with 4 collective nests. A programmable logic controller (Officine Facco & C. Spa, Campo San Martino, Padova, Italy) managed feeding, drinking, lighting, and ventilation inside the system.

The aviary housed a total of 1800 Hy-Line Brown hens (Hy-Line International, West Des Moines, Iowa, USA) in 8 pens (225 hens/pen). For the specific purposes of the present study, a 4-week trial was implemented when hens had 37-40 weeks of age. During this period, out of the eight available pens, four of them received only the commercial diet (Control group) and the remaining four received whole hemp seed (HS group) (10 % of the average daily feed intake of the whole group) once per day (10:00 am). In two pens of the HS group, hemp seeds were manually distributed in two additional circular feeders (diameter: 37 cm) per pen placed on the ground area; in the other two pens of the HS group, hemp seeds were manually distributed directly on the ground to evaluate behavioral differences according to the type of distribution (data not reported here). Then, for the specific purposes of the presents study, eggs were collected from two pens of the control group and the two pens of the HS group fed hemp seeds in the circular feeders.

During the experimental period, in the barn temperature averaged at 22.0 +- 0.5 C with relative humidity at 76.8 +- 4.8 %; hens were exposed to a 16-h light/8-h dark photoperiod and fed ad libitum the same commercial diet, based on maize and soybean meal, formulated to meet the nutritional requirements of laying hens (Hy-Line management guidelines, 2018) (Tables 1, 2).
Whole hemp seeds (mix of Futura 75 and Felina 32 var) were bought from a commercial producer (Belmais Srl., Agna, Padova, Italy) (Tables 1, 2).
Recording, sampling, and physical analyses of eggs
During the whole experimental period, the numbers of total eggs, dirty and broken eggs were counted twice per week in each pen. The egg production over the week was calculated at the pen level as:
Oviposition rate (% present hen) = total eggs at the two weekly recordings/total number of present hens at the two recordings x 100.

After 14 and 28 days of trial, 60 eggs per pen and per sampling day were randomly sampled, i.e. 240 eggs per sampling day, 480 eggs in total, to be used for assessing egg quality and immediately processed in the laboratories of the DAFNAE department.

At each sampling, whole eggs were individually weighed and candled to determine the occurrence of defects, such as pre-cracks. The egg equator diameter and height were measured using a digital caliper (IP54, SHAHE Digital Calliper, Wenzhou, Zhejiang, China). The egg shape index (SI) was calculated as SI (%) = egg equator diameter / egg height x 100. Color measurement of the shell was performed based on the CIE L* a* b* color system using a Minolta Chroma Meter CM-508 (Minolta Corp., Ramsey, NJ, USA).

Out of the 60 eggs per pen per sampling day, 30 eggs were used for texture profile analysis (TPA) and sensory analysis; the other 30 were opened, and the yolk, albumen, and shell were separated. Egg shells were oven-dried for 24 h at 50 C and weighed. After drying, the thickness of the eggshells (with membrane) was measured at 3 points (the air cell, the sharp end, the equator) using a digital caliper (IP54, SHAHE Digital Calliper). Yolk weight was measured, whereas albumen weight was calculated as the difference between the weight of the whole egg and those of yolk and dry shell. The occurrence of blood and meat spots in the yolk and albumen was visually detected. Yolk color was determined in the CIE L* a* b* color system using a Minolta Chroma Meter CM-508 (Minolta Corp.). Yolk and albumen pH were determined using a pH meter (Basic 20, Crison Instruments SpA, Carpi, Modena, Italy), equipped with a specific electrode (cat. 5232, Crison Instruments SpA).

Out of the 30 broken eggs collected per pen per each sampling day, 10 eggs were used for chemical analyses. To this purpose, 5 pools of 2 yolks each and 5 pools of 2 albumens each were made per sampling day (10 pools per experimental group) and freeze-dried to be later submitted to chemical analyses (proximate composition, fatty acids, cholesterol, and minerals).
Chemical analyses of diet, hemp seeds, yolk, and albumen

The commercial diet, hemp seeds, and freeze-dried yolk and albumen pools were analyzed for the content of dry matter (950.46), ash (920.153), crude protein (981.10), and crude fat (2003.05) according to methods. The commercial diet and hemp seeds were analyzed also for the contents of crude fiber (978.10).

For the determination of fatty acid (FA) profile of diet, hemp seeds, and freeze-dried yolk, fat was extracted by accelerated solvent extraction (ASE, Dionex, Sunnyvale, CA, USA, Application Note 334) using three extraction cycles with chloroform:methanol (2:1 v/v) as a solvent at 80 C and a 1-min heating phase and 40-sec extraction phase (as modified from). The solvent was evaporated under a N2 stream (Genevac EZ-2, SP Industries, Warminster, PA, USA) at 60 C; the residual samples (extracted lipids in vials) were weighed before adding 4 ml of 1 % H2SO4 in methanol and held at 50 C overnight. Then, hexane (1 ml hexane for 20 mg extracted fat) and 4 ml of NaSO4 (0.47 % in H2O) were added to transfer the methylated FAs in the organic phase. The organic phase was collected after centrifugation and analyzed by GC-FID with an Agilent 7820A Gas Chromatograph (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) by injecting 1 mul with a split ratio of 65:1. A Supelco OMEGAWAX-TM 250 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) (30 m x 0.25 mm internal diameter, 0.25 mum film thickness) was used with hydrogen as the carrier at 1.4 ml/min. The oven temperature was set at 50 C, held for 2 min, raised to 220 C at the rate of 4 C/min, and then held for 23 min. Both the injector and the detector temperatures were set at 250 C. The individual FA were identified by comparing the retention time of the standard FA methyl ester mixture (Supelco 37-component FAME Mix, 47,885-U). Individual FA methyl esters were expressed as the percentage of the total area of eluted FA methyl esters.

Mineral contents of diet, hemp seeds, freeze-dried yolk and albumen pools were determined on 0.30-0.35 g of sample placed in a tetrafluoro-metoxil (TFM) vessel with 2 mL of 30 % hydrogen peroxide and 7 ml of concentrated (65 %) nitric acid, both of Suprapur quality (Merck Chemicals GmbH, Darmstadt, Germany). The samples were subjected to microwave digestion (Ethos 1600 Milestone S.r.l., Sorisole, Bergamo, Italy) as follows: step 1, 25-200 C in 15 min at 1200 W with max pressure 100 bar; step 2, 200 C for 18 min at 1200 W with max pressure 100 bar; and step 3, 200-35 C in 15 min. After cooling to room temperature, the dissolved sample was diluted with ultrapure water (resistivity 18.2 M Omega cm at 25 C) to a final volume of 25 ml. The mineral contents were determined by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) (Spectro Arcos EOP, Spectro Analytical Instruments GmbH, Kleve, Germany). Calibration standards were prepared using multi- and single-element standard solutions (Inorganic Ventures Inc., Christiansburg, VA, USA) in 30 % Suprapur nitric acid (Merck Chemicals GmbH) to obtain similar matrices to the samples.

The determination of cholesterol content in egg yolk pools was performed by GC-FID analysis after saponification with methanolic KOH. Briefly, 4 ml of a solution of KOH in methanol (0.5 M) was added to 100 mg freeze-dried egg yolk and agitated in a water bath at 80 C for 30 min. After cooling the sample to the room temperature, internal standard (5 alpha-cholestane), 3.5 ml n-hexane, and 2 ml water were added and the sample was shaken vigorously. The organic phase was collected after centrifugation and analyzed by GC-FID with an Agilent 7820A Gas Chromatograph (Agilent Technologies) by injecting 2 mul organic phase with a split ratio of 60:1. A HP-5 ms column (Agilent Technologies) (15 m x 0.25 mm internal diameter, 0.25 mum film thickness) was used with hydrogen as the carrier at 1.2 ml/min. The oven temperature was set at 40 C and raised to 220 C at the rate of 4 C/min, and then held for 2 min. Both the injector and the detector temperatures were set at 280 C.
Shell strength analysis

Shell fracture test was performed on 15 eggs per pen (30 eggs per group) using a texture profile analyzer (Stable Micro System Ltd., Goldaming, UK), equipped with a cylindrical probe 30 mm in diameter at the constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/sec using a 250 N load cell.
Sensory analysis of eggs

Triangle tests with 50 panelists were conducted on different sample triplets (two eggs from the Control group and one egg from laying hens fed hemps seeds; and one egg from the Control group and two eggs from laying hens fed hemp seeds). The volunteers, students and staff members of DAFNAE, consumed three eggs coded with three-digit random numbers.

For sensory evaluation, eggs were placed in water at room temperature. Then, the water was raised to the boiling point, and the eggs were kept in the boiling water for 8 min. The eggs were cooled to room temperature, shelled, and then cut into quarters (lengthwise). Samples were served on 15-cm white paper board plate identified with a 3-digit blind code and each participant was asked to recognize the different eggs. Mineral water and unsalted crackers were provided to clean the palate between the samples.
For the ranking test, panelists were asked to rank all samples of eggs according to overall acceptability by attributing 1 for the most acceptable sample and 3 for the least acceptable one.
Statistical analysis

Data related to egg quality traits and chemical composition were submitted to analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the group (control vs. HS), the sampling day (14 vs. 28 d), and their interaction as the main factors of variability, and the pen as a random effect, using the PROC MIXED procedure of SAS. The differences in the occurrence of shell pre-cracks, blood spots, and meat spots were analyzed by the chi2 test of SAS according to the group. Differences between the means with P <= 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Proximate and mineral composition of the egg yolk and albumen were not affected by the dietary enrichment with hemp seeds (P > 0.05) (Table 5). On the other hand, the rate of total saturated fatty acids (SFA) in the yolk was lower (-2.39 %; P = 0.006) in HS hens compared to hens of the control group due to the decrease in myristic (C14:0; P = 0.011) and palmitic (C16:0; P < 0.001) acids (Table 6). The rate of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) also decreased (-7.73 %; P = 0.002) due to the lower rates of palmitoleic acid (C16:1n7; P < 0.001), oleic acid (C18:1n9; P = 0.005), and vaccenic acid (C18:1n7; P = 0.002). Conversely, both PUFA n3 (+42.9 %; P < 0.001) and PUFA n6 (+11.3 %; P < 0.01) increased, resulting in higher total PUFA rate (+15.9 %; P < 0.001) in yolk lipids of hens enriched with hemp seed because of higher rates of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, C18:3n3; P < 0.001), docosapentaenoic acid (DPA, C22:5n3; P < 0.001), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, C22:6n3; P < 0.001), and linoleic acid (LA, C18:2n6; P = 0.002). The PUFA n6/n3 ratio significantly lowered from 9.32 to 7.44 (P < 0.001) with the enrichment of hemp seeds (Table 6).

With respect to the sampling day, the rate of DHA (P = 0.034) and AA (P = 0.049) increased from day 14 of the experiment to day 28 (Table 6). Then, as for mineral composition, the contents of Na and Mg (0.05 < P < 0.001) in yolk and albumen decreased from day 14 to day 28 as it was for the content of S in the yolk (P = 0.024) (Table 7).
Sensory analyses of eggs

Concerning the sensory analyses, 46 % of the participants guessed which eggs belonged to the same experimental group, whereas the remaining 54 % were not able to discriminate between the eggs obtained from the laying hens that received hemp seeds and those of the control group (P = 0.042) (data not shown in tables). Moreover, the ranking of the eggs by the panelists showed no significant preferences for the eggs from hens enriched or not with hemp seeds. In fact, in the first triangle test, the sum of the liking scores (from 1 for the most acceptable sample to 3 for the least acceptable one) was equal to 44 and 52 for the two eggs from the Control group and 54 for the eggs from laying hens fed hemps seeds (P > 0.05); then, in the second triangle test, the sum of the liking scores was equal to 45 for the eggs from the Control group and 48 and 57 for the two eggs from laying hens fed hemp seeds (P > 0.05) (data not shown in tables).
Discussion

According to, hemp seeds contain 24.8 % crude protein and 35.5 % crude fat, with 27.6 % crude fiber and 5.6 % ash, whereas data by and the present study measured a similar crude protein content (23.8 % to 24.1 %) and a lower crude fat content (27.5 % to 30.4 %). The differences in the chemical composition of hemp seeds reported among studies are due to the different varieties, preliminary treatments, pedological and climatic situations, and agronomical practices used.

Previous studies evaluated levels of dietary inclusion of hemp seed varying from 3 % to 30 % and found that the inclusion up to 20 % of hemp seed did not impact feed intake, final bird weights, and average daily egg production. Differently, at high inclusion levels (30 % of the diet), found that hemp seeds did not affect plasma chemistry of laying hens, but decreased egg weight during the first eight weeks of production, achieving the same weight as a control egg. also reported that the high inclusion of hemp seeds (20 % and 30 % compared to 10 %) in the diets negatively affected the egg-laying performance. On the other hand, 10 % of the dietary inclusion of hemp seeds did not impair the production performances of laying hens but provided the possibility of the enrichment of yolk fat with PUFA in the study performed by. Thus, under the conditions of the present study, with whole hemp seeds provided as an enrichment over the diet distributed ad libitum, egg oviposition rate was not affected, which is in line with previous studies where 15 % and 20 % of whole hemp seeds had been included in the diets of laying hens.

In previous studies using diets containing whole hemp seeds or hempseed cakes, physical properties of eggs or yolk weight were slightly affected, as happened in the present trial. On the other hand, reported that while 10 % dietary HS inclusion (replacing the same % of soybean meal and wheat) did not influence egg weight, a 20 % inclusion rate increased egg weight, suggesting a dose dependent effect of HS inclusion.

As for the traits rather important for consumers, changes in yolk color due to pigments in raw materials used in diet formulation or used as overfeed enrichments should be considered. Whole hemp seeds supplementation could change yolk color thanks to their content of chlorophylls and carotenoids (manly lutein). However, the dietary inclusion of hemp seed cake has been found to have no effects on yolk color due to the removal of lipid components including pigments. found that the dietary replacement of soybean, sunflower, and corn oils with HS oil decreased L* and a* values of yolk, whereas reported that the dietary inclusion of 10-20 % whole HS (replacing the same rates of soybean meal and wheat) decreased L* and increased a* and b* in egg yolk. In the present trial, only L* value of yolk was significantly decreased without effects on the redness and yellowness indexes which could be attributed to a low pigment intake under the conditions of our trial, i.e. whole hemp seeds distributed at 10 % of daily feed intake to a rather large group of hens.

In our study, the yolk pH of hens fed hempseed was lower than that of the control hens. In fact, higher antioxidant capacity has been measured in eggs of laying hens fed diets containing 8 % ground hemp seed compared to those of hens fed a control diet, proportional to the higher concentration of alpha-tocopherol in the yolks, where dietary antioxidants can reduce lipid oxidation products, potentially lowering pH.

As for the nutritional composition of eggs, yolk or albumen, no effects of the enrichment with whole hemp seeds were observed in our study, as expected and previously reported, but differences in the fatty acid profile were evident. Indeed, while hemp seeds are a valuable source of various minerals, including P, K, Mg, Ca, Na, and Fe, information regarding the effects of their dietary inclusion on egg mineral composition has not been reported.

Regarding cholesterol, contrary to previous beliefs, eggs may not be associated with increased cholesterol levels and risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), but they are rather part of well balanced and healthy diet. In this regard, reported that cholesterol content in the egg yolk linearly decreased from 1925 to 1167 mg/100 g of egg yolk by increasing the dietary inclusion of hemp seeds from 0 to 25 %. The same authors suggested that hemp seeds lower cholesterol in yolk primarily through the effect of phytosterols, including beta-sitosterol, that inhibit cholesterol absorption by crystallization and coprecipitation, and its lower solubility that displaces cholesterol from intestinal micelles, reducing its absorption. Phytosterols may also lower hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis in hens by modulating the activity of enzymes, including HMG-CoA reductase, so limiting cholesterol formation. Nevertheless, under our conditions, the dietary supplementation with 10 % whole hemp seeds did not affect the cholesterol content in yolk, corroborating previous reports.

On the other hand, in our study, the FA composition of the yolk was significantly changed by the dietary enrichment with whole hemp seeds. In fact, HS fat is particularly rich in linoleic acid (LA) (>50 % of total FA), alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) (17 % to 19 % of total FA), and gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) (up to 4 %). Under our conditions, the enrichment with whole hemp seeds significantly increased the rate of the total n-3 PUFA of egg yolk due to increased ALA and DHA. These changes in FA are attributed to the high content of ALA in hemp seeds, besides the ability of hens to convert ALA to n-3 long-chain FA, via Delta 5-desaturase, Delta 6-desaturase, and elongase. In fact, unlike humans, whose capacity for synthesis of EPA and DHA is limited, hens are able to convert ALA to EPA and DHA, which is why the inclusion of sources rich in ALA in the diets of laying hens increases the deposition of these n-3 long chain PUFA in eggs.

In line with the present findings, found a significant increase in ALA, DHA, and thus total n-3 PUFA in eggs yolks when 10-20 % whole hempseed was used in the diet. The same authors also reported an increase in EPA, that we did not find in our study as it was in other studies in which laying hens were fed diets with different sources of fats rich in ALA, such as canola, sunflower, linseed, and fish oils. The absence of EPA may be due to the efficient conversion of EPA to DHA by elongation and desaturation processes in the liver of hens.

In our study, the total n-6 PUFA proportion increased in the yolk as a consequence of hemp seed enrichment mainly due to a higher rate of LA. On the other hand, arachidonic acid (AA) rate in yolks was not different according to the hemp seed enrichment, as also reported by other authors, despite the high ALA rate (as found herein) could have limited the synthesis of AA from LA, to the competition for the same Delta-6 desaturase enzymes.

The dietary supplementation with hemp seeds improved the n-6/n-3 PUFA ratio, reducing it from 9.32 to 7.44, closest to the recommended value of 4; increased total PUFA with a contemporary decrease in SFA and MUFA rates, as already found in other studies. Apart from diet, which is the major factor influencing FA composition, the increased activity of the birds due to hemp seed enrichment (data not presented in the present paper) could have also contributed to the changes in fatty acid composition of the yolk to some extent.

Despite the health benefits related to n-3 PUFA, enrichment with these FAs may lead to lower sensory acceptability in eggs, as previously reported because of the dietary inclusion of fish oil, fish meal, or flax seed. showed that different oil sources (microalgae, fish oil) affect egg sensory acceptability in a dose-dependent manner and concluded that supplementation from microalgae oil would produce DHA-enriched eggs more acceptable for consumers than when using fish oil. In fact, fish-based raw materials can transmit undesirable odors and flavors to eggs probably due to the accumulation of trimethylamine (TMA). Previous studies also reported "fishy" odors of eggs due to increased TMA deposition, when rapeseed meal was added to laying hens diet.

The meta-analysis of highlighted the need to define the optimal level of hemp seeds and hemp-seed products to be included in the diets of laying hens for improving the fatty acid composition of table eggs, where the impacts on their sensory quality has scarcely been investigated. reported that feeding laying hens with diets containing up to 20 % whole hemp seeds did not result in differences in sensory characteristics of cooked eggs compared to the control, except for minor differences in the sweet taste. In the study of, trained panelists did not find significant differences in different sensory attributes between eggs from laying hens fed the control diet and their counterparts fed a diet containing 15 % hemp seeds. The results from different studies are hard to compare because the preparation of the eggs has a role in its perception since the cooking method may affect volatile compounds. Nevertheless, under our conditions, almost half of the untrained panelists could differentiate hard-boiled eggs from different dietary treatments - without finding differences in the rank rating between samples - even if they did not detect any fishy or rancid odor and fishy off-flavor, which are in general associated with elevated PUFA content in eggs.

The changes in egg quality with the sampling day were mostly linked to the increased age of the hens. In fact, egg weight increased, shell thickness decreased, and egg shape changed on day 28 compared to day 14 as previously observed when laying hens get older. On the other hand, it is worth mentioning that while these differences were statistically significant, they were numerically small among the various quality parameters. Consistently with the results of, the present study also reported a rise in the occurrence of blood spots in the eggs with increasing age of the laying hens. Then, a small significant decrease in eggshell lightness was measured over time. In general, the color of the eggshell tends to become lighter as the hen grows older which has been attributed to an increase in egg size. Finally, under our conditions, the absence of significant interactions between enrichment with hemp seeds and sampling day implies that a two-week supplementation period may be sufficient to achieve a desirable effect on the fatty acid composition of yolk lipids.
Conclusions

The present study showed that the feeding enrichment with 10 % of hemp seeds in laying hens resulted in increased n-3 PUFA (in particular ALA and DHA), n-6 PUFA (mainly LA), and total PUFA contents in yolk lipids, more beneficial n-6/n-3 PUFA ratio, without negatively affecting egg quality, chemical composition and mineral content of eggs. Sensory analysis demonstrates that 10 % hemp seed supplementation may be used in the diet of the laying hens without adverse effects on the sensory characteristics of eggs, suggesting market potential for this product. Further insights are expected on the possible beneficial effects of such an enrichment in cage-free system for laying hens in view of increased positive welfare and decreased occurrence of welfare concerns.

passages.text: Warfarin Induced Non-Uremic Calciphylaxis

Calciphylaxis is a rare and life-threatening condition characterized by vascular calcification and thrombosis, typically seen in patients with end-stage renal disease but also associated with long-term warfarin use in non-uremic patients. We present the case of a 78-year-old woman with a mechanical aortic valve on chronic warfarin therapy who developed progressive, painful necrotic skin ulcerations over ten months. Skin biopsy confirmed warfarin-induced non-uremic calciphylaxis. Following shared decision-making, warfarin was discontinued and replaced with low molecular weight heparin, and intravenous sodium thiosulfate was initiated. This case underscores the importance of recognizing non-uremic calciphylaxis in warfarin-treated patients and highlights the need for early diagnosis, multidisciplinary management, and shared decision-making to balance the risks of anticoagulation against serious complications like calciphylaxis.

A 78-year-old female with a past medical history significant for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, aortic stenosis status post mechanical aortic valve replacement treated with warfarin for over ten years presented with painful necrotic skin ulcerations for the past ten months. The patient noted that the lesions began as erythematous migratory blistering skin lesions initially involving the ankles that evolved into necrotic ulcerations, and eventually moved to the shins, thighs, hip, buttock, and abdomen (Figures 1 and 2). Prior to her presentation, the patient was treated with multiple antibiotics along with wound care and debridement in the outpatient setting. These interventions proved to be ineffective, as the skin lesions were enlarging and spreading to new areas, prompting her visit to the hospital for a higher level of care. On arrival, vital signs were stable. A complete blood count and basic metabolic panel were both within normal limits. Prothrombin time (PT) was elevated at 26.2 sec (ref: 12.1-14.8 sec) and the international normalized ratio (INR) was elevated at 3 (ref: 0.8-1.2) in the setting on warfarin usage. Wound cultures were significant for heavy pseudomonas aeruginosa. Blood cultures were negative. Dermatology was consulted for biopsy and treatment recommendations. Biopsies revealed vascular calcium deposition associated with the deep dermis and superficial subcutaneous tissue.
Multiple irregular black eschars with peripheral erythematous halos distributed across both thighs on admission.
Sharply demarcated black eschar with peripheral erythema in the left lower abdominal quadrant on admission.

Taken together, these lesions were suggestive of non-uremic calciphylaxis in the setting of warfarin intake. Cardiology was consulted for recommendations regarding warfarin usage for prior mechanical aortic valve replacement in the setting of the newly diagnosed non-uremic calciphylaxis. The patient and her husband were very hesitant to discontinue warfarin as she was on warfarin for over a decade after mechanical aortic valve replacement. Shared decision making was done with the patient and her husband at bedside, and she was subsequently transitioned from warfarin to low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). She was also treated with intravenous sodium thiosulfate. The patient was scheduled for follow-up with outpatient dermatology after discharge; however, her hospital course was further complicated by acute hypoxic respiratory failure and she ultimately passed away shortly after.

Calciphylaxis is a rare life-threatening condition most commonly affecting patients with end stage kidney disease on dialysis. It is characterized by calcification and thrombosis of small blood vessels, leading to painful non-healing necrotic skin ulcers, which can be complicated by secondary infection and sepsis, contributing to its high mortality rate. Unlike uremic calciphylaxis, non-uremic calciphylaxis occur in patients without end-stage renal disease. It is linked to a broad spectrum of underlying conditions such as chronic kidney disease, hyperphosphatemia, hypercalcemia, hyperparathyroidism, and vascular calcification. Additional associations include coagulation disorders, aluminum toxicity and iron dextran use. Clinical reports have also suggested potential links with renal transplantation, immunosuppressive therapy, corticosteroid use, and obesity.

Warfarin, a commonly prescribed anticoagulant, has also been associated with the development of calciphylaxis. Warfarin- induced non-uremic calciphylaxis should be considered in patients with normal kidney function presenting with painful necrotic lesions in the setting of chronic warfarin usage. The lesions may initially present as livedo reticularis, reticulate purpura, violaceous plaques, or indurated nodules. Ulcerations often progress to necrotic lesions with black eschar, as observed in our patient. Regardless of etiology, calciphylaxis is associated with high morbidity due to severe pain, chronic non-healing wounds, prolonged hospitalizations, and recurrent superimposed infections. Ulcerated lesions in calciphylaxis carry a reported 1-year mortality rate of 45-80%, with sepsis being the most common cause of death.

Histopathologically, calciphylaxis is marked by microvascular thrombosis, calcification, and fibrointimal hyperplasia of cutaneous arterioles, leading to ischemia and septal panniculitis. Vascular calcification is thought to cause endothelial dysfunction and injury; however, the precise pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and optimal management of this devastating condition remain incompletely understood. Warfarin-induced non-uremic calciphylaxis presents with painful, necrotic skin lesions that are typically located on the lower extremities, particularly below the knees. Patients may experience severe pain, erythematous nodules, and plaques that can progress to ulcerations and gangrene. The condition predominantly affects females and is associated with long-term warfarin use, with an average duration of 32 months after initiation of warfarin.

Our patient has many risk factors for the development of non-uremic calciphylaxis, including warfarin use, female sex, and obesity. When considering this patient's history of chronic warfarin usage in the setting of lower extremity necrotic ulcerative lesions, and the characteristic pathology report, the most likely etiology of these necrotic lesions is warfarin-induced non-uremic calciphylaxis. The pathophysiology of warfarin- induced non-uremic calciphylaxis is driven by the relationship between warfarin and vascular calcification. Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of matrix Gla protein (MGP), a potent inhibitor of vascular calcification. This inhibition leads to increased vascular calcification of the tunica media and intima of small vessels.

Shared decision-making is essential when initiating warfarin therapy in patients with mechanical heart valves, given the serious risks of complications such as warfarin-induced calciphylaxis and the high risk of stroke with anticoagulation nonadherence. Treatment of this condition includes discontinuation of warfarin and substitution with heparin or LMWH to halt further progression of the calcifications. Sodium thiosulfate treatment is recommended for its ability to enhance calcium solubility and promote excretion. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has also been described to promote wound healing and is associated with better survival when combined with other treatments in patients with warfarin-induced non-uremic calciphylaxis. Wound care and multimodal pain management with NSAIDs and opioids are also recommended to limit potential infectious complications and mitigate the severe pain associated with calciphylaxis, respectively.

passages.text: The CALCIPHYX trial and its impact on calciphylaxis treatment: what's next?

Calciphylaxis, also known as calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is a rare vasculopathy characterized by calcium deposition in the arterioles of the deep dermis and subcutaneous adipose tissue that results in severely painful, ischaemic skin lesions. The pathogenesis of calciphylaxis is not yet fully elucidated. Medial calcification of arterioles in the deep dermis and subcutaneous adipose tissue is proposed to play a crucial role, leading to ischaemia, endothelial injury, tissue infarction, and skin necrosis (Fig. 1). Although calciphylaxis is associated with several complications (tissue necrosis, infections, sepsis, etc.) and extremely high mortality rates (40%-70% at 1 year), there are no approved therapies.

Proposed mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of calciphylaxis. (a) Typical histologic elements of a normal arteriole in the skin, including an intact endothelium, internal elastic lamina, contractile vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and elastin fibres. (b) Histologic analyses of skin samples from patients with calciphylaxis have demonstrated the presence of hydroxyapatite in the microvascular and extravascular subcutis, thereby implicating hydroxyapatite crystallization in the extracellular matrix as a key contributor to disease pathogenesis. In more detail, in the case of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and exposure to other toxins, VSMCs are likely to shift from a contractile to an osteochondrogenic phenotype, marked by increased expression of transcription factors such as runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2). These altered cells produce matrix vesicles enriched with calcium (Ca) and phosphate (PO4), which foster crystalline hydroxyapatite formation in the extracellular matrix. The propensity for arteriole calcification depends on the balance between calcification promoters (e.g. BMP-2 and BMP-4) (grey) and inhibitors [e.g. carboxylated matrix Gla protein (c-MGP), fetuin-A, and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi)] (red). Carboxylated MGP restricts BMP-induced VSMC transformation and mineralization by integrating into matrix vesicles. However, a deficiency or inhibition of vitamin K impairs MGP carboxylation, encouraging VSMC transdifferentiation and mineral deposition. This process is compounded by decreased MGP production in the transdifferentiated VSMCs, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. Adipocytes may further contribute by releasing vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A). These lead to arteriolar calcification; this combined with endothelial damage and thrombosis lead to the full-spectrum of the disease and clinical manifestations.

The management of calciphylaxis and its complications is complex, requiring a multidisciplinary, multimodal approach; this includes targeting the disease's pathophysiology with intravenous therapies while simultaneously addressing its debilitating symptoms with pain management and wound care protocols. Sodium thiosulphate is frequently used off-label, based on case reports and case series; however, a recent meta-analysis demonstrated no benefit regarding survival or healing skin lesions. Based on the proposed pathogenesis, several agents for the treatment of calciphylaxis have been tested in clinical trials. In an open-label, phase 2 trial, hexasodium fytate (SNF472), a hexasodium salt of myo-inositol hexaphosphate (IP6, phytate) was associated with improvements in wound healing, pain, and health-related quality of life.

CALCIPHYX was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase-3 trial evaluating the effects of hexasodium fytate on several efficacy and safety outcomes (Table 1). Seventy-one patients were randomly assigned to hexasodium fytate 7 mg/kg or placebo (1:1) intravenously during haemodialysis session for 12 weeks. Both arms showed similar improvements in the primary efficacy outcomes (between-group P = .88 for the Bates-Jensen Wound Assessment Tool (BWAT)-CUA and P = .15 for pain VAS). Similarly, no significant between-group differences were observed in the secondary efficacy outcomes. With regards to safety outcomes, adverse events that led to treatment discontinuation were fewer in the hexasodium fytate group (5% vs 18%); calciphylaxis-related infections (3% vs 21%), hospitalization (5% vs 33%), and death (3% vs 15%) were also lower in the treatment arm. During the subsequent 12 weeks of open-label hexasodium fytate and 4 weeks of follow-up, there were no additional calciphylaxis-related events leading to hospitalization.

The primary and secondary efficacy outcomes did not significantly differ between the two arms, so this is a negative study. The key question is: are we looking at the right endpoints that are analysed in the most informative way? First, it used two patient-centred alternate primary efficacy outcomes that had not been prospectively validated in calciphylaxis patients; these endpoints may lack sensitivity to capture potential improvements in wound healing or the effect on critical outcomes such as death and hospitalization.

Notably, deaths were numerically lower in the hexasodium fytate group (5% vs 21%). An important point to take into account is that the intention-to-treat analysis of the primary outcome did not consider competing risks. Most likely, death was not a random occurrence and individuals having more severe disease were more likely to die. Hence, given that more patients in the control group died (possibly due to the severity of the disease), this introduces a competing risk that could skew the analysis of the primary endpoint. The aforementioned discrepancy led to a higher rate of missing data in the placebo group, and, along with the trial's 12-week duration and the small sample size of the groups due to the rarity of the disease, may have affected the differences in primary endpoints.

In this context, in the post hoc, hypothesis-generating analyses of composite endpoints of time to death or hospitalization (both calciphylaxis-related and total), or days alive and out of hospital, patients randomized to hexasodium fytate showed clinically meaningful improvements that were of nominal statistical significance. The hazard ratio for death or hospitalization was 0.13 (95%CI 0.00-0.46, nominal P = .002) at 12 weeks and 0.18 (95%CI 0.00-0.55, nominal P = .004) at study-end. Rate ratios (RRs) for adjusted events rates were also lower for the hexasodium fytate at both 12 weeks (hospitalization or death, RR = 0.074, nominal P < .001; death or total calciphylaxis-related events, RR = 0.298, 95%CI 0.133-0.668, nominal P = .003) and study-end.

Overall, the CALCIPHYX was the first phase 3, placebo-controlled, randomized trial completed in patients with calciphylaxis. Although the trial did not meet either of its primary efficacy outcomes, the findings of the post hoc analyses prompt further investigation into the mechanisms of action and potential therapeutic benefits of hexasodium fytate. In addition, the trial highlights the feasibility of performing randomized clinical trials of novel treatments for this devastating disease that does not have an approved therapy yet. While the randomized, double-blind design should theoretically ensure balance in baseline characteristics, the small sample size inherent to this rare condition increases the likelihood of residual imbalances in disease severity. This is particularly important given that death in calciphylaxis is often a non-random event associated with more severe disease, introducing a competing risk that may have confounded efficacy analyses based on the intention-to-treat principle. In future studies, this risk could be more effectively mitigated through stratified randomization based on the severity of calciphylaxis at diagnosis, for example according to the abdominal or peripheral location of the lesions or the presence of an infection at the time of inclusion.

Moreover, given the multifaceted pathophysiology of calciphylaxis, it is uncertain that intravenous therapies such as SNF472 will be sufficient. Effective wound care remains essential for promoting healing, and its integration into clinical trial protocols is critical to advancing patient care. Moreover, the inflammatory and microvascular nature of calciphylaxis (Fig. 1) suggests a potential role for adjunctive anti-inflammatory therapies. Treatments aimed at reducing blood viscosity, such as rheophoresis, may potentially enhance perfusion of the micro-circulation in affected areas. Theoretically, such approaches may work synergistically with SNF472. While inhibition of microvascular calcification remains a central therapeutic target, it may not represent the most actionable mechanism in isolation. A comprehensive approach that simultaneously addresses vascular calcification, local tissue damage, and systemic inflammation may offer a more holistic and effective strategy for improving outcomes in this high-risk patient population.

passages.text: Direct ammonia and dihydroxyacetone production in an unbiased photoelectrochemical cell

Photoelectrochemical production of ammonia usually suffers from a low solar-to-ammonia efficiency and a high overpotential, which influences the bias-free operation of sustainable photoelectrochemistry. Herein, we realize solar-driven ammonia production from waste nitrate by constructing copper-osmium catalysts deposited on the Sb2(S,Se)3 semiconductor, enabling optimized photo-carrier transport pathways and a beneficial co-adsorption configuration of *NO3-H2O moieties. The photocathode reaches a photocurrent density of 5.6 mA cm-2 at 0 VRHE with a low onset potential of 0.86 VRHE and a Faradaic efficiency of 96.98% at 0.6 VRHE under AM 1.5 G illumination. We further employ glycerol oxidation reaction on ruthenium doped bismuth oxide catalyst decorated on titanium oxide photoanode, requiring an onset potential of 0.3 VRHE to enable bias-free operation. The unbiased photoelectrochemical system shows Faradaic efficiencies of over 97% for ammonia products and above 77% for glycerol oxidation product under AM 1.5 G illumination. The large-sized photoelectrodes maintain a stability for 24 h without noticeable degradation. Our works indicate that unassisted and stable PEC ammonia production is feasible with in situ glycerol valorization using the photoanode and photocathode.

Photoelectrochemical production of ammonia faces challenges with low efficiency and high overpotential. Here, the authors report a bias-free system using copper-osmium and ruthenium-based catalysts, coupled with glycerol oxidation, for solar-driven ammonia production.
Introduction

Ammonia (NH3) is the second most produced chemical globally, a key precursor for fertilizers and fine chemicals. The sustainable solar energy renders it an option for renewable energy applications. Photoelectrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (PEC NO3RR) for NH3 production is one of the promising manners performed at ambient temperature and pressure without emitting carbon dioxide. However, it suffers from low solar-to-ammonia efficiency, poor selectivity, and high onset potentials since the conversion of nitrate to ammonia involves an eight-electron transfer process. Such performance is mainly attributed to poor utilization of solar flux and slow charge transport in the photoelectrodes. Furthermore, hydrogen evolution reaction becomes competitive compared to PEC NO3RR. Also, the nitrite (NO2-) as an incomplete reduction product of nitrate poses a threat to the selectivity and yield of NH3. To address these, Fan et al. employed a ZnIn2S4/TiO2 photocathode to convert nitrate to ammonia, exhibiting a photocurrent density of 3 mA cm-2 at -0.1 VRHE. On the other hand, to advance the bias-free operation with the photoanode side for PEC system, semiconductor's onset potential must be low enough, which is a criterion for the bias-free PEC cell since applying bias increases production cost and energy consumption. Amal et al. reported a Cu2ZnSnS4 photocathode loaded with the defective TiOx cocatalyst and CdS buffer layer for PEC NO3RR, showing an ammonia yield of 8.21 micromol h-1 cm-2 at -0.2 VRHE and a Faradaic efficiency of 89.1% at 0.1 VRHE with a positive onset potential of 0.38 VRHE. Moreover, our group reported CuSn alloy catalyst decorated on the Sb2S3 photocathode with the deposition of a titanium oxide layer, exhibiting an onset potential of 0.62 VRHE. Although the low onset potential has been obtained, the current density at low potentials is not ideal, and the performance of the PEC unbiased system greatly depends on the current density at low bias potential. Therefore, developing a suitable photoelectrode and cocatalyst becomes a primary challenge in enhancing solar conversion efficiency and improving photogenerated charge utilization efficiency for potential applications.

As we know, NH3 production coupled with water oxidation requires an additional bias owing to high thermodynamic potential for water oxidation (1.23 V). To replace the traditional water oxidation reaction to produce oxygen with low economic value, glycerol oxidation reaction (GOR) has been developed to convert low-cost feedstock to high-value-added chemicals with thermodynamic equilibrium potential. Coupling a favorable anode oxidation reaction to obtain value-added products with NH3 production at the photocathode might offer sustainable applications. More recently, Si/Cu-NSTL/Co(OH)2 photocathode with a Schottky barrier contact was reported to enable optimizing photogenerated carrier transport pathways and a beneficial co-adsorption configuration of *NO3-H2O moieties. The photocathode for PEC NO3RR was then coupled with a Cu/Pt-Si photoanode for GOR to produce formate without any applied additional bias, lowering the potential requirement in comparison to that of water splitting. Jang et al. applied a triple-cation lead halide perovskite photocathode with integrated electrocatalyst to achieve high solar-to-ammonia productivity and coupled electrochemical glycerol oxidation (glyceric acid as a major value-added product) for bias-free NH3 production. Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is driven by substantial market demand and a high market value ($150/kg), establishing it as the most desirable product within GOR. It originates from secondary hydroxyl oxidation, yielding a three-carbon (C3) product within a carbon chain. The pursuit of maintaining a balanced carbon chain to produce DHA selectively is thus appealing for energy conversion. Designing a suitable photoelectrode with a low onset potential applied in PEC couplings while obtaining high value-added products remains challenging.

Herein, we developed a high-performance PEC cell using a low-cost Sb2(S,Se)3 photocathode with the deposition of copper-osmium electrocatalyst (CuOs/CdS/SSS) for selective PEC NO3RR towards efficient ammonia products. The resultant photocathode reaches a photocurrent density of 5.6 mA cm-2 at 0 VRHE with a low onset potential of 0.86 VRHE, and especially, it exhibits much higher performance in the low overpotential compared to the traditional photoelectrodes reported. In addition, we employed ruthenium doped bismuth oxide decorated on titanium oxide photoanode for glycerol oxidation reaction, requiring a low onset potential of 0.3 VRHE to enable bias-free operation. The selective CuOs and Ru-Bi2O3 cocatalysts provide improved stability and selectivity with low onset potentials in acid electrolytes. The CuOs/CdS/SSS photocathode coupled with a GOR photoanode show Faradaic efficiencies of over 90% for NH3 production and above 77% for GOR under AM 1.5 G illumination without applying any potential. Furthermore, the large-sized photoelectrodes maintain a stability for 24 h without noticeable degradation, representing one of the notable performances among bias-free PEC cells for high value-added products reported so far. This work motivates development for producing value-added products from low-value/waste compounds.
Results
Characterization of CuOs/CdS/SSS photocathode
Characterization of CuOs/CdS/SSS.

The CuOs/TiO2/CdS/Sb2(S,Se)3 photocathode was fabricated via a two-step hydrothermal approach, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Briefly, an Sb2S3 seed layer was firstly prepared on a fluorine-doped tin oxide substrate using a hydrothermal method. Afterwards, Sb2(S,Se)3 absorber layer was formed in a second hydrothermal process in a selenourea precursor. The film formed a gradient doping of Se enriched at the bottom during the reaction. A CdS layer as a transfer layer was deposited on the top surface of Sb2(S,Se)3, following by the deposition of an amorphous TiO2 protective layer (noted as CdS/SSS). Finally, the copper-osmium-based cocatalyst was decorated on the CdS/SSS, and the sample is denoted as CuOs/CdS/SSS. For comparison, the Cu cocatalyst deposited on the CdS/SSS photocathode was synthesized (labeled as Cu/CdS/SSS). The morphology structures of the relevant photocathodes were observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The pristine SSS and CdS/SSS show a dense grain with a size of ~500 +- 100 nm (Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2). The CuOs catalyst exhibits a nanoparticle structure on the surface of CuOs/CdS/SSS (Supplementary Fig. S3), similar to that of Cu/CdS/SSS (Supplementary Fig. S4). The layered structure of the electrode is clearly shown in Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. S5. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image exhibit the thicknesses of 700-800 nm for the light-absorbing layer with a Se-rich layer of ~300 nm. The interface between CuOs, TiO2, CdS, and Sb2(S,Se)3 can be evidently observed (Fig. 1c). The lattice spacing for the CuOs catalyst is measured to be 0.182 nm corresponding to the (200) plane of Cu (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. S6), and Sb2(S,Se)3 presents the lattice spacing of 0.302 nm assigned to the (211) plane of Sb2S3 (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. S7).

All the photocathodes exhibit the crystal structure of Sb2S3 (JCPDS No. 73-0393) in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Supplementary Fig. S8). In the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), the peak at 932.1 eV in the Cu 2p spectra and the peaks at 564.4 eV and 566.1 eV in the Cu LMM spectra represent the metallic states of Cu on both Cu/CdS/SSS and CuOs/CdS/SSS, the presence of Cu+ and Cu2+ can be associated to oxidation caused by exposure to air (Fig. 1g, h and Supplementary Fig. S9a, b). The Os 4 f spectrum shows an oxidation state at 52.6 and 56.6 eV, which suggests surface oxidation of the photoelectrodes due to air exposure (Fig. 1i and Supplementary Fig. S9c). Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) elemental mappings obtained from the cross-sections of CuOs/CdS/SSS exhibit that Cu and Os elements are distributed on the surface of the semiconductor, and Se is detected at the bottom of the film with a thickness of around 300 nm (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Figs. S10-S12). The band gaps of the pristine TiO2, CdS, and Sb2(S,Se)3 based on the absorption edges of the UV-vis spectra are 3.2, 2.55, and 1.75 eV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S13). Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy determines the energy band structure of the photoelectrodes (Supplementary Fig. S14). The layered heterostructure of TiO2, CdS, and Sb2(S,Se)3 result in a series of step like conduction band shifts (Supplementary Fig. S15), effectively suppressing interface charge carrier recombination and promoting charge transfer.

We measured the PEC NO3RR performance of the photocathodes in an H-cell in 5 mM H2SO4 and 0.1 M KNO3 (pH=2) under AM 1.5 G illumination without iR correction. As shown in Fig. 2a, no evident photocurrent density for the photocathodes can be observed under dark conditions. Under one sun illumination, the pristine SSS shows a low photocurrent density of -1.57 mA cm-2 at 0 VRHE. CdS/SSS and CuOs/CdS/SSS display enhanced photocurrent densities under tested potential range, -3.37 mA cm-2 and -5.6 mA cm-2 obtained at 0 VRHE, respectively. Cu/CdS/SSS exhibits a similar photocurrent density with the CuOs/CdS/SSS at the potential range from 0.4 to 0.8 VRHE. Importantly, the onset potentials of Cu/CdS/SSS and CuOs/CdS/SSS are considerably shifted to the positive values of 0.84 VRHE and 0.86 VRHE, respectively, which are lower than those of SSS (0.42 VRHE) and CdS/SSS (0.63 VRHE) (Supplementary Fig. S16). This proves that the decoration of Cu or CuOs cocatalyst facilitates the nitrate conversion. The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves of all photocathodes in the absence of NO3- show the lower photoresponses (Supplementary Fig. S17) in comparison to the photocathodes in the presence of NO3-, which denotes the positive PEC NO3RR activity of the photocathodes. Note that CuOs/CdS/SSS reaches a photocurrent density of -0.26 mA cm-2 at 0.1 VRHE compared to the Cu/CdS/SSS (-0.17 mA cm-2) in the electrolyte without the addition of NO3-. The increase in hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity of CuOs/CdS/SSS could be correlated with the ability of Os cocatalyst to adsorb hydrogen protons.

Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) and ammonia yields were evaluated through an indophenol blue approach (Supplementary Fig. S18). As displayed in Fig. 2b, CdS/SSS exhibits an ammonia FE of 35.6% at 0.1 VRHE, and FE decreases as the potential shifts to the positive direction, indicating that its slow charge carrier dynamics impedes the conversion of NO3- to NH4+. Although CuOs/CdS/SSS and Cu/CdS/SSS display a similar photoresponse (Fig. 2a), there is a noticeable difference in ammonia FE. Cu/CdS/SSS has an FE of 70.4% at 0.1 VRHE, accompanied by a decrease with potential. In contrast, CuOs/CdS/SSS depicts an averaged ammonia FE of ~90% over the potential range from 0.1 to 0.8 VRHE, reaching a maximum value of 96.98% at 0.6 VRHE. The partial photocurrent density of CuOs/CdS/SSS for NH4+ synthesis (JNH3) is -4.28 mA cm-2 at 0.1 VRHE (Supplementary Fig. S19), almost consistent with the LSV curve (Fig. 2a). This high FE on CuOs/CdS/SSS can be attributed to distinct PEC NO3RR behaviors between Cu/CdS/SSS and Os/CdS/SSS, in which Os/CdS/SSS has shown enhanced FEs with increasing the applied potential owing to facile PEC NO3RR kinetics on the Os sites (Supplementary Figs. S20 and S21). In Fig. 2c, CuOs/CdS/SSS displays the highest NH4+ yield among these photocathodes, reaching 19.87 mumol h-1 cm-2 at 0.1 VRHE, which is higher than the Cu/CdS/SSS (15.10 mumol h-1 cm-2) and CdS/SSS (2.25 mumol h-1 cm-2). CuOs/CdS/SSS exhibits a maximum NH4+ selectivity of ~98% (Fig. 2d), notably higher than Cu/CdS/SSS (55.8%) and CdS/SSS (38.9%). These results suggest the improved PEC NO3RR kinetics on the sulfide-based photocathodes by the deposition of CuOs catalyst. In addition, NH4+ yield and FEs are also influenced by the concentration of nitrate sources. CuOs/CdS/SSS shows that ammonia yield raises from 1.18 to 5.67 mumol h-1 cm-2 with an average FE over 96% as the NO3- concentration increases from 10 to 200 mM (Fig. 2e). This indicates that the photoelectrode could maintain high selectivity of active hydrogen in NO3RR process over a wide range of nitrate concentration, enabling efficient intermediate hydrogeneration.

We also compared the electrocatalytic properties of the Cu and CuOs catalysts (Supplementary Fig. S22). Cu and CuOs catalysts exhibit comparable current densities in the LSV curves. Cu shows a FE of 37.5% at 0.2 VRHE and its FE gradually increases to 72.4% at -0.2 VRHE, while CuOs maintains an average FE of ~90% in the potential range from -0.2 to 0.2 VRHE. Ammonia selectivity has demonstrated that CuOs achieves high selectivity at more negative potentials, reaching a selectivity of 95% with a yield of 2.1 mmol h-1 cm-2 at -0.2 VRHE. Cu catalyst displays inferior ammonia selectivity compared to CuOs, consistent with the results on the CuOs/CdS/SSS for PEC NO3RR. The electrocatalytic NO3RR is operated continuously for 24 h at 140 mA cm-2 without obvious performance degradation, indicating a stable property of the catalyst toward NO3RR.

NO2- as the main by-product seriously influences the hydrogenation process of NH4+ reduction, and we thus examined the PEC NO2- performances for the corresponding photocathodes (Supplementary Fig. S23). Except for CdS/SSS, Cu/CdS/SSS produces a large amount of NO2- at the measured potentials. To confirm the origin of NH4+ and the accuracy of the ammonia yield, we analyzed the N source in NH4+ by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy using isotopically labeled N15O3- (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. S24). No characteristic peaks of N15H4+ are detected in the fresh electrolyte before NO3RR measurement (bottom right as illustration in inset of Fig. 2f). After the reaction, the typical 1H NMR double peaks corresponding to the N15H4+ are observed in the electrolyte, suggesting that the detected N15H4+ is derived from N15O3- reduction rather than from environmental N contamination. The yield and FE of NH4+ determined by 1H NMR are consistent with the colorimetric method, which verifies the reliability of the experimental results (upper left as illustration in inset of Fig. 2f). The catalytic activity and product yield of CuOs/CdS/SSS were further investigated during a long-term operation. The photocathode exhibits stable photocurrent densities at 0.6 and 0.4 VRHE for 6 h, and its FEs remain an average value of 93% and an accumulated yield of 78.8 mumol cm-2 during 12 h (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. S25). Furthermore, the sample maintains stable ammonia yields and FEs in 20-cycle testing (Fig. 2h), suggesting the stable property of the photocathode toward PEC NO3RR.

We employed intensity-modulated photocurrent spectroscopy (IMPS) to determine the photocathode's charge transfer rate and charge recombination rate. The rate constant of the maximum phase shift at the apex of the semicircle in the third quadrant represents charge transfer rate (Ktran) and charge recombination rate (Krec) (Supplementary Fig. S26). The semicircles in the second and three quadrants of IMPS plots reflect the competition between interfacial charge carrier transfer and recombination, and the relation of charge carrier and relaxation in the photoelectrodes. The charge transfer efficiency [ktrans/(ktrans+krec)] is obtained by calculating the steady-state and instantaneous photocurrent densities. In the potential range of 0.6 to 0 VRHE, the surface recombination of Cu/CdS/SSS and CuOs/CdS/SSS are completely suppressed (Supplementary Fig. S27). Also, in conjunction with the frequency at the maximum imaginary value in the IMPS plot, we analysed the rate constants (ktrans+krec) for charge transfer (ktrans) and recombination (krec). The trend of ktrans is CuOs/CdS/SSS   Cu/CdS/SSS > CdS/SSS (Fig. 2i, j), consistent with the above PEC activities, indicating that the photocarriers can be rapidly transferred from semiconductor to the surface reactions for CuOs/CdS/SSS or Cu/CdS/SSS. The surface co-catalyst promotes the release of photogenerated charge to the reactants by lowering the potential barrier of NO3RR. Moreover, CuOs/CdS/SSS has shown the highest electrochemical active surface area (Supplementary Fig. S28) and the lowest resistance (Fig. 2k) among these photocathodes.

Recently, the PEC oxidation of glycerol (GOR) to dihydroxyacetone (DHA) has received increasing attention. TiO2 exhibits inherent advantages, including stability in acidic media and a favorable onset potential, making it particularly suitable for integration with the present photocathode. Although the wide bandgap and the limited light absorption capacity of TiO2 limit its theoretical photocurrent density, we synthesized the TiO2 photoanode with the decoration of Ru doped Bi2O3 cocatalyst (noted as Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2) since Bi2O3 can enhance the visible light absorption of TiO2. XRD pattern confirms the crystalline structure of anatase TiO2 (JCPDS No.21-1276) (Supplementary Fig. S29). SEM and TEM images exhibit a one-dimensional nanorod structure of TiO2 (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. S30). The nanoparticles with a size of 40-50 nm are covered on the top surface of sample (Fig. 3b, c), with a d-spacing of 0.316 nm corresponding to the (201) plane of Bi2O3 (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. S31). The Bi and Ru elements are also reflected by the Bi 4 f and Ru 3 d XPS peaks (Supplementary Fig. S32). TEM elemental mappings exhibit Bi and Ru species decorated on the TiO2 nanorod (Fig. 3e).

We next compared the LSV curves of TiO2 and Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 for PEC GOR in 0.5 M Na2SO4 (pH=2, adjusted by H2SO4) with or without 0.1 M aqueous glycerol solution under AM 1.5 G illumination. Both TiO2 and Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 exhibit higher photoresponses in the presence of glycerol than those in the absence of glycerol (Fig. 3f), suggesting a lower reaction energy barrier for glycerol oxidation than water oxidation. Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 exhibits an enhanced GOR performance compared to the pristine TiO2, with a photocurrent density of 2.81 mA cm-2 at 1.2 VRHE. Ru-Bi2O3 can serve as an efficient photosensitizer to enlarge the optical absorption to the visible light region. Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. S33 show the FEs over TiO2 and Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 within 1 h quantitatively analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography. TiO2 produces a large amount of formic acid (FA) with a FE of 23.1% and a selectivity of 41.3% at 0.6 VRHE (Supplementary Fig. S34). After the Ru-Bi2O3 deposition, the FE of FA product decreases, while C3 products, including DHA and glyceraldehyde (GLD) increase, especially for the considerable increment of DHA with a FE of 42.9% and a selectivity of 59.2% at 0.6 VRHE. For the total C3 products, including DHA, glyceric acid (GLA), and GLD, Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 has yielded a higher total FE of 62.9% than TiO2 (26.2%) at 0.6 VRHE (Supplementary Fig. S35). Figure 3h depicts the DHA yields and selectivities for the Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 under a wide potential window of 0.4 ~ 1.2 VRHE. The increase in potential leads to a decrease in DHA selectivity, while the DHA yield gradually increases owing to the increase in photocurrent density, reaching a maximum value of 18.84 mumol cm-2 h-1 at 0.8 VRHE. We also evaluated the FEs and yields of products for the Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 at various potentials (Fig. 3i and Supplementary Fig. S36). As the potential increases, the FE of C1 product (FA) increases, while the FEs of C3 products (DHA, GLA, GLD) decrease. In addition, the overall FEs for GOR gradually decrease with increasing the potential, from 81.13% (0.4 VRHE) to 70.25% (1.2 VRHE) (Supplementary Fig. S37). The photocurrent density of Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 remains unchanged at 1.2 VRHE over 20 h, accompanying with the relative stable FE values (Fig. 3j). It is generally considered that a high DHA selectivity would be difficult to obtain under glycerol conversion owing to over-oxidation of DHA via C-C bond cleavage. In this work, the Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 photoanode can offer high selectivity of DHA.

Since the intersection of working curves on both photocathode and photoanode in a three-electrode system displays the ability to realize unbiassed operation, 1.65 mA cm-2 obtained at 0.51 VRHE (Fig. 4a), we integrated CuOs/CdS/SSS photocathode with Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 photoanode to realize unassisted NH3 and C3 production. The system consisted of two photoelectrodes connected by a copper wire in a two-compartment reactor, as depicted in Fig. 4b. The unassisted PEC system on the CuOs/CdS/SSS ll Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 shows the stability with the photoresponse of ~1.4 mA cm-2 for 10 h under AM 1.5 G illumination (Fig. 4c). The total FEs of GOR remain above 77%, and the FEs of PEC NO3RR show an average value exceeding 90% during 10 h testing (Fig. 4d). The yields of NH3 and C3 (DHA, GLD, and GLA) products increase with time, and the accumulated yields of NH3 and C3 reach 55.12 mumol cm-2 and 132.52 mumol cm-2 after 10 h (Fig. 4e), respectively. We also prepared the photoelectrodes with a large-size of 6 cm2. The coupling system exhibits a high current of ~6.55 mA with a stable operation of over 25 h (Supplementary Fig. 38). This provides a potential application of unbiased PEC synthesis for directly converting solar energy into high-value-added chemicals.

Moreover, we evaluated the economic viability of the PEC device in the unbiased system based on the market price of the products (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Tables S1-S2). The unbiassed system produces 112.08 mmol of DHA per hour under light illumination per square meter, and achieves 60.7 mmol of conversion from nitrate to NH3. The product revenues are $151 x 10-2, and the raw materials have increased in value by nearly 624.5 times their original value. The system drives the overall reaction only by solar without other energy consumption, producing high-value-added chemicals. We also performed a preliminary economic analysis to quantify the economic and the competitive edge analysis. Benefits of using this technology in a modeled 50 m2 each of anode and cathode. The methodology used is an ideal analysis and does not take into account the cost of associated operating, sales, and equipment depreciation. When only considering the values of the produced chemicals in their average price (Supplementary Table S1) and the operating costs, the proposed process shows a potential to be profitable up to about $117,000 per year for this modeled plant (Supplementary Table S2). The largest revenue and cost come from the produced DHA, catalyst preparation, and product separation, respectively. The annual consumption of glycerol and the annual production of DHA are about 2.45 ton and 1.47 ton, respectively.

The on-line differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS) and in situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) were conducted to explore the underlying reaction mechanism and detect the intermediate species generated on the photocathodes during PEC NO3RR under light illumination. Figure 5a display the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) signals on the CuOs/CdS/SSS recorded as a function of time while performing 5 tests at  intervals (each test involves a i-t scan at 0.6 VRHE). It can be seen that m/z signals at 46, 30, 31, 33, and 17 are observed, corresponding to the NO2, NO, NOH, NH2OH, and NH3, respectively. Based on in situ FTIR measurements in Fig. 5b and c, the peak at ~1095 cm-1 can be associated to the NO3- reactant in the electrolyte. At 0.8 VRHE, close to the onset potential of LSV curve, the peak of *NO2 appears at ~1241 cm-1, representing the formation of nitrite on the Cu/CdS/SSS from nitrate reduction. This peak intensity increases with increasing the applied potential to a more negative range. The peak related to *NH appears at 1432 cm-1, and the characteristic *NOH peak appears at 1365 cm-1. With the potential moving from 0.8 VRHE to 0.3 VRHE, the small peak at 1125 cm-1 can be observed, ascribing to -N-O- stretching vibration of hydroxylamine (NH2OH), which is a key intermediate for NH3 formation. Note that these hydrogenation intermediates appear at more positive potentials on CuOs/CdS/SSS compared to the Cu/CdS/SSS, confirming the rapid hydrogenation kinetics of CuOs catalysts for nitrogen-oxygen intermediates. Besides, a series of weak peak related to the *NO signal is shown at ~1589 cm-1 on Cu/CdS/SSS, while these are not be observed on CuOs/CdS/SSS. Instead, the peak at 1645 cm-1 attributed to *H2O can be observed on CuOs/CdS/SSS, which comes from the oscillation of the H-O bond during the *H2O dissociation process, implying an effective detachment of *H from H2O and facilitating the NH3 production through transferring to nitrogen-oxygen intermediates.

We also examined in-situ Raman spectra of the Cu or CuOs electrocatalysts toward NO3RR. As shown in Fig. 5f, all the catalysts exhibit two Raman bands within the potential range of 0.4 to -0.1 VRHE. Namely, the vibration mode of aqueous NO3- centers at 1049 cm-1, and the peak contributed by NO3- adsorption (*NO3-) centers at 1357 cm-1. These indicate the strong adsorption ability of NO3- on the surfaces of Cu and CuOs for the comparable NO3RR activity of Cu-based catalysts. As the potential decreases, the Raman band at 1204 cm-1 associated to the NO2 adsorption (*NO2) appears at 0.3 VRHE, indicating that *NO2 intermediates are directly introduced into ammonia production at this potential. This peak gradually decreases with decreasing the potential, and then disappears at -0.1 VRHE for CuOs. In addition, the Raman band at 1140 cm-1 associated to the nu2(NH3) appears simultaneously at 0.3 VRHE with the *NO2 signal on the CuOs catalyst, where the nu2(NH3) peak appears at 0.1 VRHE on the Cu catalyst. This indicates that adding Os can initiate the reaction process of the Cu catalyst from NO2 to NH3 at a lower potential. To assess the amount of H radical (*H) produced or consumed during PEC NO3RR, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis was implemented using 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) as the radical trapping reagent. In the absence of nitrate (Fig. 5d), Os/CdS/SSS and CuOs/CdS/SSS exhibit similar but stronger DMPO-*H signals than Cu/CdS/SSS (nine characteristic peak intensity ratios of 1:1:2:1:2:1:2:1:1), denoting that *H preferentially adsorbs onto Os or CuOs sites compared to Cu sites. In the presence of nitrate (Fig. 5e), the DMPO-*H signal is barely detectable on CuOs/CdS/SSS. This evidences that the generated *H at the CuOs/CdS/SSS surface is rapidly consumed in the hydrogenation of surface-active nitrogen-containing intermediates, producing enhanced ammonia yields and FEs.

Moreover, Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was implemented to investigate the role of Ru-Bi2O3 on TiO2 for PEC GOR (Fig. 5g). Isopropanol and n-propanol were used to distinguish the adsorption of middle and terminal hydroxyls on the catalyst surface during glycerol oxidation. The bands at 2979 and 2885 cm-1 correspond to the methyl symmetric (nu (CH3)) and asymmetric (nu (CH2)) stretching modes, respectively. The adsorption of isopropanol on TiO2 or Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 leads to a wavenumber shift to the negative shift in the C-O stretching mode (nu (C-O)) from 1164 to 1162 or 1158 cm-1. This implies the bond breaking owing to the adsorption of the hydroxyl group of isopropanol to the surface on TiO2 or Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2, especially that Ru-Bi2O3 is more conductive to the adsorption of hydroxyl groups of glycerol. On the contrary, for n-propanol adsorption (Supplementary Fig. S39a), the characteristic nu(C-O) band shifts to a lower wavenumber on TiO2, greater than that on Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2, suggesting that Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 has weaker adsorption for n-propanol. TiO2 prefers to adsorb the terminal hydroxyl position, while Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 tends to adsorb the intermediate hydroxyl group, providing an extremely favourable prerequisite for the generation of intermediate ketone groups in dihydroxyacetone. Moreover, by simulating and analyzing the adsorption of ketone-based products on the electrode using acetone (Supplementary Fig. S39b), Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 has a weakened tendency to adsorb acetone compared to TiO2, which means that DHA is more easily desorbed on Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 rather than further oxidization. The adsorption process of isopropanol on Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 was further examined by in situ FTIR under illumination. As shown in Fig. 5h, the intensities of two signals at 1731 and 1347 cm-1 gradually increase over Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 after adsorbing isopropanol, which corresponds to the formation of the carbonyl group (C O) and carboxyl group (O C-O). The appearance of the C O bond originals from the formation of acetone by isopropanol oxidation, and the O C-O bond is due to the C-C cleavage of isopropanol. Among them, the weak O C-O bond signal indicates that C-C cleavage is inhibited, demonstrating high selectivity of C3 products on Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2. In contrast, the high intensity of C O band implies high selectivity of Ru-Bi2O3/TiO2 towards ketone species.
