Discussion

For the first time, the treatment status and clinical outcomes associated with ERT in patients FD in South Korea were determined, targeting almost the entire population of FD in the country. Descriptive statistics of treatment status are presented in as much detail as possible. As a result, representative clinical outcomes were closely examined and important risk factors for each outcome were analyzed. This study is the first to cover almost all FD patients in South Korea using the NHIS with National Health Examination Data. Findings of this study have significant implications for real-world clinical practice.
Diagnosis of FD in South Korea

In this study, the average age at which FD diagnosis was made was earlier in males than in females (36.7 +- 15.2 years vs. 48.9 +- 16.0 years P < 0.001, Table 1). The age of FD diagnosis was comparable to that of the Fabry Registry (1,765 patients enrolled in December 2005, with 54% males) for males (mean age: 36.5 years), but earlier diagnosis was observed in females in the Fabry registry (mean age: 40.8 years).

Such observed discrepancies in the age of diagnosis among females between our data set (the Korean data set) and the Fabry registry do not indicate a delay in the diagnosis of FD in females in South Korea. In accordance with Korean legislation, children are not permitted to be included when using NHIS data. Consequently, patients below the age of 20 at the time of data curation were excluded from this study (Supplemental Table S1). Among patients diagnosed with FD at a young age, only those who reached the age of 20 at the time of data curation were included in the analysis. This might be the reason for the discrepancy in the age of diagnosis of FD in females between the Korean data set and the Fabry registry. Furthermore, patients diagnosed recently in a pediatric department might have been underrepresented in our data set. However, in this study, two-thirds of the patients were diagnosed in the Deparment of Internal Medicine, comparable to the finding of a previous study.
Treatment of patients with FD in South Korea

Characteristics of treatment status for FD in South Korea were inferred from the results of real-world clinical practices. Initially, nearly 90% of patients were treated with intravenous agalsidase-beta or -alpha (Table 1), despite the burdensome nature of ERT due to its intravenous route and biweekly frequency. This is because migalastat is currently a secondary treatment option for FD in South Korea. Since migalastat is a secondary treatment option, none of the patients were eligible to commence treatment with migalastat (Table 1, Supplemental Table 3).

Furthermore, the time interval between the diagnosis of FD and the initiation of ERT was relatively brief in South Korea, with a duration of two months for males and three months for females (Table 1). This suggests that it is important to include FD as a differential diagnosis when practitioners encounter CHD, CVD, or CKD in young patients. As an earlier commencement of ERT has a positive impact on clinical outcomes, it is crucial for clinicians to be aware of the importance of suspecting FD and performing diagnostic tests.

passages.text: Involvement of heart and brain in patients with FD in South Korea

Primary clinical outcomes, namely CHD, CVD, and ESKD, are summarized in Tables 3 and 4, and 5, respectively. It was noteworthy that CHD was more prevalent in females than in males. Given the pathogenesis of FD, it was anticipated that complications would be more prevalent in males. Especially, males with classic FD show a higher rate of major cardiovascular events than non-classic FD and female FD patients. Indeed, male patients exhibited a higher prevalence of CHD at an earlier age than in female patients both prior to and following FD diagnosis. Specifically, the mean age before FD diagnosis was 47.6 +- 12.0 in males and 58.7 +- 11.1 in females, while that after FD diagnosis was 35.7 +- 14.5 in males and 48.1 +- 15.0 in females (Table 3). Thus, we sought to elucidate underlying causes of the unexpected higher prevalence of CHD in female patients with FD such as genotype-phenotype differences in South Korea.

The crude HR for males on CHD was 1.56 [95% CI: 0.95-2.57] or 1.95 [95% CI: 1.41-2.70], based on aforementioned models (Table 7). The impact of ERT was not included in Model 1, as this model did not utilize administration of ERT as a covariate. In Model 2, the effect of ERT was too high to permit estimation of the HR (Supplemental Table S2). This might be attributed to the fact that all patients in Model 2 ultimately exhibited clinical outcomes. After adjusting for other covariates, being a female was identified as a risk factor for CHD in models 1 and 2, but not in model 3 (Table 7, Supplemental Table S2). However, ERT has a beneficial effect on patient outcomes. The results should indicate a decreased HR rather than an increased HR. The result of Model 3 was more likely to reflect real-world scenarios, as evidenced by the adjusted HR of ERT, which was 0.37 [95% CI: 0.24-0.57] (Supplemental Table S2). Additionally, results of model 3 indicated that CHD was prevalent in both sexes, showing no clear sexual predominance (HR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.73-1.53, (P = 0.778). Interestingly, young age was identified as a risk factor, which might be attributed to the earlier onset of CHD in patients with the classic phenotype.

In 2021, 393 patients underwent ERT for FD (unpublished NHIS data), representing more patients than the number of patients observed in the present study (N = 228). The discrepancy between the two data could be attributed to the exclusion of patients with an age below 20 at the time of data curation who were not eligible for enrollment. These excluded patients might have exhibited a male gender and a classical phenotype given the early onset of FD. When these excluded patients could be considered together, results might be concordant with those previously observed. In South Korea, reimbursement for ERT became available for all ages in February 2014, whereas previously it was only available to those aged between 16 and 65 years (Supplemental Table S3). As a consequence of this insurance policy, the identification of patients with FD was slower in South Korea than in other countries, which might have influenced results of our study.

The observed incidence of CVD outcomes was less than anticipated. This could be due to the fact that the ICD-10 code for CVD outcomes was I63. Codes for cerebral small vessel disease, the most frequent form of neurologic manifestations in FD, were not included. The average age of CVD was significantly younger in male FD patients than in females after FD diagnosis (40.2 +- 8.1 years in males vs. 52.7 +- 6.6 years in females, P < 0.001, Table 4), although CVD occurred in both sexes without sexual predominance. Results of the survival analysis indicated that there was no statistically significant effect of sex on CVD outcomes (adjusted HR for males, 1.07 [95% CI: 0.54-2.09]), which was similar to findings for CHD (Table 7).
Involvement of kidney in patients with FD in South Korea

Renal outcome was investigated utilizing of a specific code for ESKD and the eGFR slope derived from the National Health Examination data. It was noteworthy that a considerable number of patients were diagnosed with ESKD prior to being diagnosed with FD (21 males vs. 1 female, as detailed in Table 5). Although the age at which ESKD was diagnosed was slightly older than that observed in previous report, the younger age of dialysis initiation suggested that these patients progressed to ESKD due to FD. Because the genotype and the type of these patients (classic vs. late-onset) were not available, the cause of the difference in age of ESKD could not be determined. Moreover, the eGFR slope was found to be more rapid in males than in females, with a mean value of -2.55 ml/min/1.73m2 per year in males (P < 0.001) and - 0.09 ml/min/1.73m2 per year in females (P = 0.835), as illustrated in Fig. 2. The severity of proteinuria was not available, as the National Health Examination employed a urine dipstick analysis to measure proteinuria semi-quantitatively, which could not allow for a precise determination of proteinuria levels.

The interval between the diagnosis of FD and the commencement of ERT was relatively brief in South Korea (median 75 days in males and 103.5 days in females, Table 1). This indicates that there are few obstacles to the initiation of ERT in South Korea. Nevertheless, the high number of ESKD patients prior to diagnosis implied a lack of awareness of FD, particularly among nephrologists. A previous study demonstrated that, in South Korea, the mean duration from the onset of symptoms to FD diagnosis was approximately 10 years in adult males, compared to 1.5 years in pediatric males. The involvement of kidney in FD could be neglected, as proteinuria and slightly elevated serum creatinine are often erroneously considered indicative of chronic glomerulonephritis rather than FD. Given that ERT is less effective in patients with advanced CKD (characterized by lower eGFR and severe proteinuria), early detection of FD is critical. Furthermore, the observation of a higher mortality rate in patients who have already developed ESKD prior to FD diagnosis (Fig. 3) highlights that alpha-GLA activity and lyso-GL-3 levels should be considered in young patients with CKD with a family history. Among 897 patients receiving renal replacement therapy, 10 patients exhibited abnormal alpha-GLA enzyme activity or elevated lyso-GL-3, and one adult female was diagnosed with Fabry disease.

passages.text: The present study has several limitations. First, the genotype was unknown due to the reliance on insurance claims data. The NHIS only had laboratory data that was performed in the general population for the diagnosis of early metabolic diseases and included body mass index, waist circumference, blood pressure, serum glucose, creatinine, and urine dipstick analysis. No clinical information was available on how the disease is diagnosed or how it progresses. For example, alpha-GLA levels, quantitative urine albumin measurements (albumin-to-creatinine ratio or 24-horr urine albuminuria), electrocardiogram, and echocardiography were not available. Therefore, the type of Fabry disease (classic vs. non-classic) could not be determined in our study. Although these limitations exist, it should be emphasized that in South Korea, all treatments for Fabry disease are strictly controlled by a national committee under the centralized NHIS, ensuring that our study accurately captured nearly all adult patients receiving ERT nationwide. Second, we were unable to adjust for the degree of proteinuria in this study. As mentioned earlier, only urine dipstick results were available, preventing the adjustment of our analysis based on the degree of proteinuria. Additionally, the legal age for enrollment of patients was below 20 years at the time of data collection, which further constrained the generalizability of our findings given that the FD is a genetic disease. Despite of these limitations, this study is notable for its comprehensive investigation of the treatment of FD and its outcomes in the Korean population with nationwide perspectives. Moreover, our results underscore the necessity for a multidisciplinary approach in managing patients with FD. Fortunately, medical education programs on FD for primary care physicians and a neonatal screening program were initiated in South Korea in 2024. Future studies incorporating genotype and biochemical data including biochemical data are needed, particularly to assess untreated patients and clarify natural disease progression, especially in cases involving genetic variants of uncertain pathogenicity.
Conclusions

We investigated ERT status and outcomes for FD patients in South Korea using data from the NHIS covering nearly all FD cases in the country. Nearly 90% of patients initially received intravenous agalsidase-beta or -alpha, with migalastat available only as a secondary treatment. Our study found that males were diagnosed with FD earlier than females. We also identified a higher prevalence of cardiovascular and renal complications in males. The higher prevalence of ESKD before FD diagnosis underscored the importance of improvements in clinician awareness for early diagnosis of FD. Given the higher mortality rate observed in patients with FD and accompanying ESKD, the necessity to improve awareness of FD is highlighted to facilitate its early diagnosis.

passages.text: Manuskript zweier Linzer Apotheker aus dem Jahre 1529 mit Anweisungen zur Verhutung und Behandlung der Pest

Wenige Jahre nach Druck (1521) der ersten Pestordnung in den Habsburgischen Landern, aber ganz unabhangig davon, berichten zwei Apotheker in Linz an der Donau, Oberosterreich, in einer 32-seitigen Handschrift uber verschiedene Krankheiten, dabei aber ganz ausfuhrlich uber Vorkehrungen, die fur den einzelnen Menschen zur Verhutung einer Infektion mit der Pest zu unternehmen sind. Es wird dafur die Einnahme von speziellen Latwergen und von Zubereitungen verschiedener Pflanzen, insbesondere aus deren Wurzeln, empfohlen. Wenn jedoch die ersten Zeichen der Erkrankung bereits aufgetreten sind, ist ein an bestimmten Korperstellen gesetzter Aderlass sinnvoller. Die Angaben wie lange ein solcher noch erfolgreich sein kann, sind an mehreren Stellen des Manuskripts unterschiedlich mit zwei bis 24 h angegeben.

Das umfangliche Manuskript dient offensichtlich, anders als die Pestordnungen, nicht der Anleitung fur Obrigkeiten zur Erhaltung der Volksgesundheit, sondern die Autoren haben wohl fur Laien, Arzte und Bader geschrieben.

Im 16. Jahrhundert begann die verwaltungsmassige Bekampfung der Pest in den Habsburgischen Erblanden durch die Erstellung von Pestordnungen. Als erster Furst liess Erzherzog Ferdinand1 ,,Ein nutzliche ordnug vnd regimet wider die Pestilentz durch Doctor Hansen Saltzman vo Steir", seinem Leibarzt, erstellen, die am 15. September 1521 ,,zw nutz der Ersamen Lanndschafft" fur Graz und ganz ,,Innerosterreich" (Steiermark, Karnten und Krain) erlassen wurde. Im Jahr 1534 folgten die ,,Oberosterreichischen Lander"2 mit der in Sterzing erlassenen ,,Ordnung in den sterbenden Leuffn der Pestilentz". Wien und die ,,Niederosterreichischen Lander" (Osterreich ob und unter der Enns) erhielten 1540 ihre Anordnung ,,Wie man sich zu zeiten der Pestilentz fursehen vnd erhalten mog". Das damals von Osterreich noch unabhangige Furstliche Erzstift Salzburg betonte 1547 in seiner ,,Ordnung zu abstellung der vnsaubrigkait, hie in der Stat" die Wichtigkeit der Sauberhaltung der Orte, damit nicht ,,sonnderlichen in den Sterbennden Leuffen" [Pest] ,,pose Krannckhaiten entspringen".

Die in den Pest- oder Infektionsordnungen verlangten Massnahmen gegen die Seuche betrafen vorwiegend Vorkehrungen gegen den Ausbruch und die Ausbreitung der Seuche. An erster Stelle stand die Vermeidung der Kontakte, insbesondere mit Erkrankten und die in der fruhen Neuzeit stark vernachlassigte Sauberkeit nicht nur der Menschen selbst sondern auch ihrer Umwelt. (Genaueres uber die Pestordnungen des 16. Jahrhunderts fur die gesamten Habsburgischen Lander siehe bei Flamm).
Titelblatt der Handschrift

Die Pestordnungen haben sich an die offiziellen Institutionen gewandt, die sich fur die Gesundheit der Bevolkerung einsetzen mussten. Es erschien mir daher als angenehmer Zufall, dass ich durch die freundlichen Bemuhungen von Herrn Franz Siegle, Antiquar in Tubingen, eine Handschrift aus dem Jahre 1529 erwerben konnte, die vom Maister Paulsen, Appotekher zu Lintz, und vom Appoteckher Dominicus zu Lintz verfasst war (Abb. 1). Sie tragt den Titel ,,Regement vnd Artzneu in dem Englisch Schwais - 1529 - Vnd am lesten steet fur die Breun   Ich noch zu lest fur die Pestelentz   Vnd noch am blat ain Costlich bewart stuckh vom Hanfsamen alten vnd jungen vnd vergifften sachen" (Breun, Prein, (Hautige) Braune = Diphtherie). Die Handschrift besteht aus 38 durch einen Faden gebundenen Blattern von ca. 15 x 20 cm und zwar aus einem Titelblatt, 30 Blattern mit beidseitigem Text, einem einseitig beschriebenen Blatt sowie sechs freien Blattern.

Beide Apotheker sind weder in Linz an der Donau noch, nach schriftlicher Auskunft, in Linz am Rhein nachweisbar. Es ist aber als sicher anzunehmen, dass beide Herren im osterreichischen Linz an der Donau tatig waren. Bereits am Anfang des Manuskripts [p. 4] steht, dass die verabreichte Artzneu bei ,,kindsblatern" [Feuchtblattern], den ,,bosen Laupsilonff" [Pest] und dem ,,Englischen Schwaiss" im Welschlandt [Welschtirol = Trentino] geholfen hat. Es wird auch uber eine versuchte Behandlung von ,,Sandt vnd griess" in ,,der blatter" [Harnsteine] beim ,,ro. kn. [rom. konigl.] Postmaister zupsilon Wien" berichtet [p. 14]. Des Weiteren erfahrt man bei der Besprechung von Schutzanhangern, dass der bereits in obiger Einleitung als Initiator der ersten Pestordnung in osterreichischen Landen genannte Konig Ferdinand sich uber solche Schutzmittel informiert hat und sie offenbar auch selbst benutzt hat [p. 58]. Aus der Erwahnung Ferdinands als Konig ergibt sich die Zeit zwischen 1526 und 1561.

Die Autorenschaft der vielen einzelnen Abschnitte ist nicht angegeben. Eine Auskunft gibt das erste Blatt in der Uberschrift ,,Im Schwaiss   Regiment von Maister Paulsen. Appotekher Zu Lintz" mit Anweisungen fur das Verhalten von Kranken, die an Englischem Schweiss litten (uber Englischen Schweiss siehe Flamm).

Der folgende namentlich von Apoteckher Dominicus verfasste Text behandelt neben der Pest noch verschiedene Krankheiten wie u. a. die ,,Prein" [Diphtherie], ,,die Wurmb im Leib der Kinder", ,,Schwindtel", das ,,Bluetten [Bluten] der Nasen", die ,,Podagra" [Gicht], das ,,Zendwee" [Zahnweh], ,,Wantzen", den ,,krawit baumb" [Wacholderbaum], die ,,Rebarbara wurzen" [Rhabarberwurzel] und die ,,Ruehr" [Ruhr]. Weiters findet man in dem umfangreichen Manuskript keine Hinweise auf die Autorenschaft der einzelnen Abschnitte.
Eine Abschnittsuberschrift

Hier will ich insbesondere die in den Abschnitten ,,In der Pestilentz - Artzeneu vom Dominicus Apoteckher zu Lintz, In Ihr Jahr geschicht" (p. 3, Abb. 2), ,,Fur die Pestilentz" [p. 9], ,,Regiment fur die Pestilenz" [p. 10] und ,,Vnderricht der Lass vnd Artzeney contra Peste" [p. 35] sowie in einzelnen Abhandlungen des Manuskripts gebrachten Angaben vereinen. Diese enthalten zum Teil einander widersprechende Angaben, was wohl auf die Zusammenarbeit zweier (oder mehrerer) Autoren hinweist.
Vorbeugung der Erkrankung
Der ,,Vnderricht der Lass3 vnd Artzeney contra Peste" beginnt mit einer allgemeinen Bemerkung, ,,wie sich der Mensch in den gemainen Lauf4 halten solt, mit Arzeney vnd mit Weissheit".

Ganz wichtig fur jedem Einzelnen war die Verhutung der Pest-Erkrankung bereits zu der Zeit ,,dieweil der sterb wart", also bereits vor Auftreten der ersten Krankheitsfalle. Aus den sich sehr oft wiederholenden Beschreibungen ist allerdings nicht immer klar, ob der Text die Vorbeugung, die Behandlung oder beide betrifft.
Benediktenkraut. Vietz FB. 1800.1. Band, Tab. 43. (Die Abb. 3, 4, 5, 6 und 7 wurden freundlicherweise von der Osterreichischen Nationalbibliothek, Wien, zur Verfugung gestellt)

Neben der Vermeidung des Kontakts mit Kranken werden verschiedene Gegenmassnahmen empfohlen. Eine einfache ist, jede Nacht ein Pulver aus der Wurzel von ,,Pabstkraut genant Corda Benedicta" [Benediktenkraut = Nelkenwurz, Geum urbanum] in Essig einzunehmen (Abb. 3).

Auch die Wurzel des Teufelsabbisses [Succisa pratensis] ist zur Vorkehrung ,,guet in disen leuffen". Dazu wird die Wurzel, in einigen Rezepturen die ganze Pflanze, im Morser zu einem ganz feinen Pulver zerrieben und dieses durch ein Tuch gesiebt und in ein Glas mit bestem Wein gegeben. Von dem nach etwa einem halben Tag klar gewordenen Wein soll man dann taglich morgens nuchtern ,,einen gueten trunckh machen, vngefehrlich [ungefahr] ain claines becherlain volss".

Aber auch ,,alle Morgen nuchtern einen Trunkh Hanifmilch [Hanf-Milch] gethan, hilft davor, sonderlich ainigen leuthen", die Pest zu bekommen. Hanf wurde in der Zeit zur Behandlung und Vorbeugung bei verschiedenen Krankheiten verwendet. So empfiehtl der eingangs erwahnte Appotekher Maister Paulsen, man soll den an ,,Englischem Schweiss" Erkrankten zur Behandlung ,,auch haniff milch zetrinkhen geben"

Man kann aber auch Kranabet por [Kranabitbeeren, Wacholderbeeren] vorbeugend gegen Pest verwenden, z. B. indem man sie ein- bis zweimal in der Woche morgens in Essig zerstossen in einer sauren Speise isst. Wacholderbeeren werden auch als Latwerge (latwerge, latwerje (mhd.) = breiige Arznei, Mus) verwendet. Wer morgens nuchtern die Latwerge zu sich nimmt, ist 24 h lang sicher vor der Krankheit und sogar auch wenn er Kranke besucht. Es wird auch empfohlen, taglich die Latwerge und ein Stuck Zitwer-Wurzel [Artemisia cina, eine Beifussart] zu sich zu nehmen.
Diptam. Vietz FB. 1800. 1 Band, Tab. 75
Tormentilla. Vietz FB. 1800. 2. Band, Tab. 218
Kronwicke. Vietz FB. 1817. 5. Band, Tab. 439b

Die Herstellung einer besonderen Pest-Latwerge ist wesentlich aufwendiger: In ein Ei macht man ein kleines Lochlein, durch welches das Eiklar entfernt wird. Zum verbliebenen Dotter gibt man ungestossenen Safran und verschliesst das Loch mit einer anderen Eischale. Dann legt man das Ei zu einem Feuer und lasst es langsam braten bis die Schale uberall ganz braun geworden ist. Nach Zerstossen des Eies in einem Morser gibt man dieselbe Menge ,,weissen seniff" [Senf, Sinapis alba] dazu und nach Verarbeitung zu Pulver weiters noch je ein Lot [1 Lot = 16 2/3 g] von gestossener Wurzel des ,,weissen Tuptans" [Weisser Diptam, Dictamnus albus] und der Tormantilla [Fingerkraut, Blutwurz, Tormentilla erecta] sowie Kraut von Cronaigl [Bunte Kronwicke, Coronilla varia] (Abb. 4, 5 und 6). Alles wird zu besonders feinem Pulver zerrieben. Danach wird die Masse eventuell je nach Rezept mit verschiedenen Zugaben versehen und mindestens zwei weitere Stunden im Morser zerrieben bis eine Latwerge entsteht, die zah am Pistill hangen bleibt. Diese Latwerge halt sich in einer Buchse bis zu dreissig Jahre ,,guet vnd crefftig". Ob man diese Latwerge auch zur Verhutung der Pest oder erst nach deren Beginn geben soll, ist nicht ersichtlich.

Manche Menschen trugen zur Verhutung von Krankheiten verschiedene Amulette an einer Schnur oder Kette um den Hals. Soweit diese Hohlkorper waren - seien es kostbare Geschmeide oder nur einfache Nussschalen - wurden sie mit magischen Abwehrmitteln gefullt, die zum Teil Dufte ausstromten, weswegen sie auch Bisamapfel genannt wurden. In der Handschrift wurde empfohlen, den ganzen Tag einen Anhanger mit Teufelsabbiss ,,am blossen laib an dem herzen" zu tragen. Dafur wurde ein wenig [von dem oben beschriebenen Wein oder vom Wurzelpulver?] in ein Wachstuch und daruber in Atlasgewebe und Samt eingebunden, ,,damit das gifft gas nicht heraus mag vnd wol verwart sey", denn ,,ain gifft das andere [Gift] nicht leiden mag" lasst kein Gift zum Herzen. ,,Das hat sich [sic] konig Ferdinand, sambt anderm abgeschribenem, getraulich gebraucht".

Zusatzlich oder auch unabhangig von solchen Vorkehrungen empfiehlt es sich, vor dem Schlafengehen in einer Kammer mit versperrten Fenstern und Turen Kranabitbeer-Latwerge und Wermutkraut [Artemisia absinthium] in eine Pfanne zu verbrennen und den Rauch durch Mund und Nase einzuatmen. Am Morgen soll man dann nicht lang nuchtern bleiben, denn dies ware schadlich.

Ein anderes Rezept fur ,,Ain Rauch" sagt: ,,nimb Lorber, Cronibeten [Wacholderbeeren] vnd Wermuth clain geschnitten auf ain gluot, rauch in allen Zimmern offt damit, vnd das die Zimmer vermacht saind, damit der Rauch darin blaib".
Am Beginn der Krankheit

,,So den menschen die saich [Seuche] ankhumbt", wenn also die Seuche beim Einzelnen beginnt, so gibt man die Latwerge zerrieben und verdunnt zu trinken, und zwar alten Menschen im Gewicht eines Dukaten [3,49 g], jungen Menschen und Frauen im Gewicht eines Rheinischen Guldens [= Gewicht von drei Viertel eines Dukatens]. Dies muss spatestens in der elften Stunde nach Krankheitsbeginn geschehen, denn danach geht das Gift zum Herzen und es wurden die Latwerge und auch das Schwitzen nicht mehr helfen. Trotzdem muss man es aber auch noch spater versuchen.
Engelwurtz. Vietz FB. 1800. 1. Band, Tab. 18

Man kann aber auch in Wasser stark zerriebenes Gerstenkorn und Dukatenkraut [Habichtskraut, Hieracium] zu trinken geben. Es konnen auch uber Tag Weisser Diptam, Angelica [Engelwurz, Angelica archangelica] (Abb. 7) und Weinkraut [Weinraute, Ruta graveolens] in Essig eingenommen werden.

Wenn die Pest mit Kalte beginnt, so gibt man einen loffelvoll von der in Weisswein zerriebenen Latwerge zu trinken. Fangt die Krankheit aber mit Hitze an, so nimmt man ,,blaues Vairlwasser [Veilchenwasser] oder Wegward wasser" [Gemeine Wegwarte, Wilde Zichorie, Cichorium intybus]. Man kann auch in Essigwasser oder in frischem ,,Prunnwasser" [Brunnenwasser] zerriebene Latwerge verabfolgen.

Den Kranken legt man in ein Bett ,,vnd dekht Ihn auf das allerwermist zue, dass er schwiz, 3, 4 oder 5 stund oder noch lenger, ie mehr ie besser, dan [denn] das Gifft der Pestilenz muss sich im schwizen verzehren vnd hinweckh gehen, dann [wenn] so eins also lang schwizt, so ist er genossen [genesen]. Wolt oder nicht aber der siech [Sieche] nit schwizen, so lass von stund 4 Zieglstain warmen, vnd schlag umb ieden ein Nass tuech, leg ihm zween zu den fussen vnd zween zwischen die Pain oder an iede seithen ainen, damit er schwiz, anders genest er nicht".

,,Wan der krankh schwizt, soll man sich huethen vor seinem adem, vnd dem dampff so von Ihm gehet, damit niemand vergifft werd, man sol auch das Peth vndt Pethgewandt [Bettzeug] schon waschen vnd lang erlufften lassen."
Wenn man einen Kranken besuchen will, soll man zuvor morgens nuchtern die Latwerge essen, denn das hilft sicher 24 h lang vor einer Ansteckung.
Der Kranke selbst soll acht Tage lang kein Fleisch essen und keinen Wein trinken, ,,wolte er aber des weins nit gerathen, der ihm doch fast schadt ist [schadet], so misch ihm den mit wasser".

Will der Mensch sicher sein, dass er nicht an der Pest stirbt, so nehme er Solomey5, Bosualda, Holunderbluten und weissen Imber ((mhd.) Ingwer) und zerstosse sie zu einem Teig und trinke dies in gutem Wein.
Der Aderlass
Neben oder anstelle der ,,medikamentosen" Therapie wird auch der Aderlass angewendet. Die Angaben daruber finden sich an verschiedenen Stellen des Manuskripts und sind widerspruchlich.

Wenn sich bei einem Menschen Zeichen der Pest zeigen, so soll er zur Ader gelassen werden, und zwar in einer Angabe spatestens nach zwei Stunden, in einer anderen innerhalb von 12 h, denn danach ,,ist das Siechthumb volkommen vnd hilfft dan kain arznay nicht mehr" und der Mensch muss sicherlich sterben. An anderer Stelle wird angegeben, dass man 24 h nach Auftreten der ersten Zeichen beim Menschen nicht mehr zur Ader lassen sondern purgieren soll. Es ist darauf zu achten, dass niemand schlaft, bevor er zur Ader gelassen wurde oder eine Latwerge eingenommen hat.

Nun sollt man wissen, ,,alles Gifft kumbt von dem Luft [mask.!] so er vergifft ist". Die Luft vergiftet den Menschen, zerstort ihn und bringt den Tod. Das Gift der Luft geht zuerst in die Hand und dann zum Herzen. Dieses wird ,,todtlich" und sendet das vergiftete Blut zu den Achseln. Wenn es dort nicht hinauskann, geht es zur Leber und danach ins Hirn. So werden dem Menschen drei ,,Haubt glider ganz zerstort vnd sein Natur [wird] krankh vnd bringt dem menschen den Todt".

Wenn also ,,am menschen ain zaichen [der Krankheit] vnder den Ichsten [Achseln]" auftritt, ,,so ist das Herz krankh in den Todt". Wollte man dem Herzen zu Hilfe kommen, so lasst man auf der Hand des gleichseitigen Arms zur Ader, ,,die da haist die herz adern". Machte man dies am anderen Arm, brachte dies zweifachen Schaden: gutes Blut wurde ,,aussgegossen" und bei einer abermaligen Erkrankung wurde an der [dann?] gesunden [derzeit kranken?] Stelle vergiftetes Blut ,,aussgegossen". ,,So wird dann das blut ganz zerstort zu baiden saithen", wodurch das Herz stirbt. Demnach soll man immer nur auf dem Arm zur Ader lassen, neben dem das Zeichen aufgetreten ist.

,,Erhebt sich aber ain Zaichen bei dem gemacht [mannl. Genitale] zu nechst bei der Haimblichkait der scham, so sollt Ihr wissen, dass die Leber krank und vergiftet ist. Dann sollt Ihr auf demselben Fuss lassen, und zwar auf der Ader, die zwischen grosser und der nachsten Zehe geht, und nicht auf dem Arm, denn das Gift wurde zum Herzen oder zum Hirn gezogen und brachte den sicheren Tod."

,,Erhebt sich dann ein Zaichen hinden von der scham (schame (mhd.) = Scheu, Rucksicht, Genitale) und erscheint an den diech [Schenkel], so solt Ihr auf demselbigen fupsiloness lassen", und zwar auf der Ader zwischen den kleinen Zehen. Wenn ,,es auch sticht in saiten", so lasst ,,auf der Baslica und der Latain Bathica und auch auf der Ader, die da heisst Salucela und zwischen dem mittleren und dem langen Finger verlauft".

,,Erhebt sich aber ein Zeichen unter den Ohren oder unter dem Kinn, so sollt Ihr auf der gleichseitigen Hand lassen, insbesondere auf der Ader, die da Zevalica heisst und uber der medianen Ader auf der Ader zwischen Daumen und Zeigefinger liegt".

Der Kranke darf nur kurz schlafen, denn kommt er uber zwolf Stunden, so hilft das Lassen nicht mehr. ,,Wer vergifft ist mit dem siechthumb der blatern" [hier: Pestwunden] und/oder ,,driesen" [Drusen, hier angeschwollene Lymphknoten] soll z. B. Senfsirup, Holunderbluten und Krauter-Essig einzeln oder in Mischungen auflegen.
Im Manuskript findet man mitten zwischen anderen Abschnitten auch eine Kurzanleitung fur die Auswahl der jeweiligen Stellen zum Aderlass [p. 22]:
,,Nemblich so ainem ain zaichen auffart, soll alweg auf derselben saithen gelassen werden, da das zaichen ist.
Also war es under den iachsen [Achseln], so lass die Media an derselben saithen mitn auf dem armb.
Ists beim gemachten, so lass die ross ader.
Ists auf den lendten, so lass bei der klain zehen.
Ists am knie, so lass die haubt ader beim daumen.
Ists beim orn, so lass auch die haupt ader beim daumen.
Ists auf der Ichsel [Achsel] oder auf dem Nackhen, so lass die ader baim clainn finger."

Es werden auch Anweisungen gegeben, ,,wie man sich in dem Lauff halten soll, mit Essen, damit man sich mit der hilff Gottes vor der Plag bewahren mogt". Man soll frische, jedoch nicht zu hart gekochte Eier essen, etwas Fleisch von jungen Lammern und jungen Ziegen, auch sonst gebratenes junges Fleisch, ausser vom Schwein, aber auch Wildbret und Fische aus fliessenden Gewassern. Alles soll ungesalzen sein, denn ,,gesalzens ist gifft". Dazu kann man auch ,,klaren, nicht zu alten, nicht zu jungen" Wein trinken, aber nicht zu viel Wasser.

Solche Empfehlungen fur die Ernahrung zu Pestzeiten gab es bereits acht Jahre vor der Handschrift, namlich in der Pestordnung von 1521 fur Innerosterreich. Es ist jedoch anzunehmen, dass diese den beiden Apothekern in Linz nicht bekannt war. Fur das Herzogtum Osterreich ob der Enns mit dem Hauptort Linz wie fur das Herzogtum Osterreich unter der Enns findet man die ersten Angaben fur ,,Speyss vnd Trannckh" in Pestzeiten erst in der Pestordnung fur die Niederosterreichischen Lander von 1540. Die Essensvorschlage beruhen wohl auf eigenen Erfahrungen der Autoren und denen von Kollegen und von Badern und Arzten.

Das umfangliche Manuskript der beiden Linzer Apotheker mit auch manchen einander widersprechenden Empfehlungen zur Vorbeugung und zur Vermeidung der Pest enthalt nicht wie die Pestordnungen die Anordnungen fur Massnahmen lokaler Obrigkeiten, sondern ist wohl fur Behandler und vielleicht auch fur gebildete Laien bestimmt.

Der am 10.03.1503 in Alcala de Henares, Spanien, geborene Ferdinand erhielt bei der Habsburgischen Erbteilung die osterreichischen Erblande und war somit ab 1521 deren Regent, er wurde 1526 Konig von Bohmen und Ungarn, 1531 Romischer Konig und nahm 1556 als Kaiser den Namen Ferdinand I. an. Er starb am 24.07.1564 in Wien.

Die ,,Oberosterreichischen Lander" waren Tirol und die ,,zugetanenen und inkorporierten Herrschaften vor dem Arl und Fern" sowie die osterreichischen Vorlande (Letztere sind die Herrschaften in Oberschwaben = Vorderosterreich sowie die Herrschaften im Elsass und im Breisgau).

Der ,,Lass", das ,,Zur-Ader-lassen" kommt von lazen, lan, lozen [mhd.] = u. a. (zu)lassen, geschehen lassen, erdulden; als gebrauchliche Kurzform wird ,,Lassen" gebraucht (als Substantiv und als Verb); der Aderlasser wird auch Lassl, Lassel genannt.
Von louf, lof, loefel [mhd.], Leuff = Lauf, Bewegung, Ereignis; fur Seuchen oft als ,,gemeine" oder ,,sterbende" Laufe auch Sterbleuff, vielfach auch speziell fur die Pest gebraucht.

passages.text: Association between the dietary index for gut microbiota and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
Background

Nutrient interactions with the gut microbiome modulate the development of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and cardiovascular disease. The dietary index for gut microbiota (DI-GM) is an innovative and comprehensive diet index to assess quality for health of gut microbiota.
Method

This is a cohort study from the interview date to the date of death or the end of follow-up (December 31, 2019). Involving 13,390 participants in National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), including 3538 with MASLD and 9852 without MASLD. DI-GM was calculated using 14 foods and nutrients with clear positive or negative impacts on gut microbiota, and MASLD was assessed based on liver steatosis and cardiometabolic risk factors, with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality determined through probabilistic matching and death certificate review. Restricted Cubic Spline (RCS) analysis and Cox regression were palyed for the DI-GM-mortality correlation. Subgroup analyses to identify the interactive factors that influence their relationship in MASLD. Six sensitivity analyses reinforced findings.
Results

MASLD participants exhibited lower DI-GM levels, which were statistically associated with higher mortality. Each DI-GM unit increase in MASLD was associated with a 13% lower all-cause mortality (HR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.98) and a 19.5% lower cardiovascular mortality (HR = 0.805, 95% CI 0.690-0.938). In advanced fibrosis MASLD, this increase was linked to a 20% lower cardiovascular mortality risk (HR = 0.800, 95% CI 0.691-0.927). Age and prediabetes significantly modified DI-GM's effect on mortality risk.
Conclusions

The study revealed a significant inverse correlation between the DI-GM and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality in patients with MASLD, which provide dietary suggestions and guidance for MASLD patients in preventing early mortality. However, limitations such as the cross-sectional design, potential residual confounding, and population-specific generalizability should be considered when interpreting these findings.

Introduction

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a common chronic liver disease, has grown significantly over three decades, imposing a major healthcare burden. In particular, its global prevalence surged 50% from 2005 to 2020 and may affect half of the US population by 2040. This new terminology was developed from earlier concepts, such as Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD), which has limitations, as it relies on exclusion criteria and fails to capture the underlying pathophysiology. In 2020, Eslam et al. proposed a new term, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Fatty Liver Disease (MAFLD), which encompasses a spectrum of liver diseases associated with metabolic disorders, emphasizing the metabolic abnormalities underlying fatty liver disease. Nevertheless, concerns remain regarding the heterogeneous etiology of MAFLD and the potential stigmatizing language associated with its terminology. Recently, through a Delphi consensus process involving global experts, MASLD was recommended as an alternative to MAFLD. The change from NAFLD to MAFLD/MASLD is not solely a nomenclature change, but it is acquiring a more comprehensive scope over a multi-organ metabolic dysfunction rather than a disease solely associated to an abnormal liver ultrasound imaging. It has been shown that MAFLD can be a better predictive and prognostic diagnosis compared to NAFLD in cardiovascular adverse events. MASLD's diagnostic criteria are less restrictive compared to MAFLD's rigid requirement of two metabolic risk factors, as it allows the use of any single risk factor that is supported by easily accessible data. Currently, cardiovascular mortality has surpassed liver-related deaths as the leading cause of mortality among patients with MASLD. MASLD highlighting metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular risks, expanding the scope to a broader population, emphasizing cardiovascular risk factors, and providing enhanced flexibility in assessing the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), thus improving the awareness and management of CVD risk. Despite prevalent use of outdated terms, this study adopts the new terminology.

MASLD represents a spectrum of liver diseases characterized by hepatic steatosis (fat accumulation) driven by metabolic dysfunction, independent of alcohol consumption. Its pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of metabolic, inflammatory, environmental, and dietary factors et al.. While extensive understanding has been gained regarding the dietary mechanisms underlying MASLD, the role of the gut microbiota in its pathogenesis remains poorly understood. The intestinal microbiome, an intricate ecosystem encompassing bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses, resides symbiotically within the human body. Notable alterations in the gut microbiome and disruptions of the gut-liver axis (GLA) contribute substantially to the pathogenesis of human MAFLD. Additionally, the gut microbiome plays a multifaceted role in cardiovascular health, with microbial dysbiosis acting as a common trigger in the pathogenesis of both MAFLD and CVD.Dietary factors and alterations are pivotal in shaping the composition of the microbiota. MASLD is now known to have both genetic and environmental risk factors. It has been shown in the last 15 years that several gene variants are closely associated with hepatosteatosis, the most important of which being PNPLA3. Diet is one of the key environmental risk factors influencing the development of MASLD. Therefore, the manipulation of dietary habits to cultivate a healthy gut microbiota has emerged as both effective and economical intervention for MASLD patients. While numerous dietary indices are currently available, their associations with indices of gut microbiota diversity and richness are not uniform.

To address this gap, Bezawit E. Kase and colleagues developed the dietary index for gut microbiota (DI-GM) through a systematic review of interventional and longitudinal observational studies, identifying 14 food items and nutrients that significantly influence the gut microbiota. The DI-GM comprises 4 detrimental ones (e.g., refined grains, and high-fat diets) and 10 beneficial foods (e.g., fermented dairy products, fiber), which collectively enhance alpha and beta diversity indices, increase concentrations of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate and acetate, and modulate the Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio.

The DI-GM stands out as a scientifically robust and innovative tool, offering a comprehensive and specific assessment of diet-gut microbiota interactions. Importantly, the DI-GM fosters interdisciplinary collaboration, bridging nutrition, microbiology, medicine, and epidemiology to advance our understanding of diet-microbiota-host interactions. Previous research has demonstrated the broader implications of DI-GM, linking higher scores to reduced biological age, lower incidence of depression, and alleviation of specific symptoms, underscoring the profound influence of a gut microbiota-health diet on overall human health.

Specifically, DI-GM incorporates key nutrients and food components with well-defined mechanistic roles in modulating gut microbiota and disease outcomes. For example, Dietary fiber (e.g., from whole grains, vegetables, and fruits) acts as a prebiotic, promoting the growth of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus while enhancing short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production (e.g., butyrate, acetate). These SCFAs improve intestinal barrier integrity, reduce systemic inflammation, and modulate lipid metabolism, thereby mitigating hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular risk. Fermented dairy products (e.g., yogurt, kefir) introduce probiotic strains that restore microbial balance, suppress pathogenic bacteria, and enhance anti-inflammatory cytokine production. This dual action reduces gut permeability and systemic endotoxemia, which are critical drivers of both MASLD progression and CVD development. Polyphenol-rich foods (e.g., berries, tea, dark chocolate) act as postbiotics, modulating microbial fermentation patterns to increase SCFA production and reduce oxidative stress. These effects are linked to improved insulin sensitivity and reduced atherosclerosis risk. These mechanistic insights underscore the importance of DI-GM in capturing diet-microbiota interactions that directly influence MASLD and CVD outcomes.

Despite these advancements, the association between DI-GM and mortality risk in MASLD patients remains unexplored. Given the gut microbiome's dual role in the pathogenesis of MASLD and cardiovascular disease (CVD), we hypothesize that DI-GM may serve as a pivotal indicator for mitigating mortality risk in this vulnerable population. This study seeks to address this critical gap by investigating the relationship between DI-GM and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality in MASLD patients. By doing so, it aims to provide evidence-based dietary recommendations for maintaining gut microbiome stability and designing targeted interventions to counteract the mortality risks associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis in MASLD.
Method
Study participants

NHANES is a US health and nutrition survey of civilians, combining interview and physical exam data. Methodologies are detailed in separate publications. The survey includes demographics, socioeconomic factors, diet, and health status. Approved by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) Ethics Board, the study adheres to STROBE guidelines and used data from 2007 to 2018 cycles. Pregnant individuals were excluded due to the potential confounding effects of pregnancy on metabolic and hepatic parameters, as well as the unique physiological changes in the gut microbiome during gestation. Participants with missing MASLD data were excluded because the primary outcome of this study (MASLD status) relies on accurate diagnosis via liver steatosis and cardiometabolic risk factors. Incomplete data on these key variables would compromise the validity of our analysis. The population was 30,786 individuals aged >= 20, excluding pregnant individuals (n = 347), those with missing MASLD data (n = 17,032), or inadequate follow-up (n = 17), leaving a final sample of 13,390 (9852 non-MASLD, 3538 MASLD) (Fig. 1).
Definition of DI-GM

Drawing from the research conducted by Kase et al., a total of 14 food items or nutrients were identified as constituent elements of the DI-GM. These included avocados, broccoli, chickpeas, coffee, cranberries, fermented dairy products, fiber, green tea, soy, and whole grains, categorized as beneficial components. In contrast, red meat, processed meat, refined grains, and high-fat diets (constituting >= 40% of energy from fat) were classified as detrimental components. The DI-GM scoring system employs gender-specific medians to account for inherent differences in dietary patterns, nutrient metabolism, and gut microbiota composition between males and females. Studies have shown that sex differences influence dietary intake (e.g., protein, fiber, and fat consumption) and microbial diversity, which may affect the relationship between diet and disease outcomes. Using gender-specific medians to reduce potential confounding and improve the accuracy of DI-GM as a proxy for gut microbiota health in each sex. For beneficial foods, participants whose intake exceeded the gender-specific median were assigned a score of 1, whereas those with intake below the median received a score of 0. Conversely, for detrimental foods, a score of 0 was assigned to participants with intake above the gender-specific median, and a score of 1 to those with intake below the median. The DI-GM score was computed by summing the scores from each component, resulting in a range of 0 to 14.
Definition of MASLD and advanced fibrosis

Fatty liver index (FLI) score >= 60 is diagnosed as steatotic liver disease (SLD). Participants with were excluded adhering to the Delphi procedure to meet the diagnostic criteria for MASLD. Finally, MASLD is defined as SLD that is co-existent with at least one cardiometabolic risk factor. Exclusion criteria and cardiometabolic risk factor were provided in the Supplementary Methods.

For the assessment of advanced fibrosis, we utilized three non-invasive scoring systems: the NAFLD fibrosis score (NFS), the fibrosis-4 (FIB4) score, and the aspartate aminotransferase to platelet ratio index (APRI). A patient was considered to have advanced fibrosis if at least one of these scores indicated a high probability of advanced fibrosis. The specific cut-off values for these scores were provided in the Supplementary Methods.
Outcomes and covariates

NHANES data were linked to the National Death Index (NDI) to determine survival status through probabilistic matching and death certificate review, which can calculate all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Causes of death were categorized using the Tenth Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10). All-cause mortality was defined as deaths occurring due to any etiology. Cardiovascular mortality was defined as fatalities resulting from primary cardiovascular disorders (e.g., ischemic heart disease, heart failure) and cerebrovascular events, categorized under ICD-10 codes I00-I09, I11, I13, I20-I51, and I60-I69. The time to event, measured in months, was computed from the date of the NHANES interview to the date of death or the conclusion of follow-up (December 31, 2019), whichever came first.

In addition to the primary outcomes, a comprehensive set of potential confounding factors was gathered and included as covariates in the analysis. These covariates encompassed age, sex, race/ethnicity, education level, marital status, poverty income ratio (PIR), presence of prediabetes mellitus (preDM), history of CVD, and cancer, as well as measures of energy intake, physical activity and alcohol consumption. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) as well-established markers of hepatocellular injury and hepatic inflammation, which are central to the pathophysiology of MASLD.

Statistical analyses

To uphold NHANES analysis integrity, we adhered to NCHS weighting guidelines. We calculated weighted means (+- standard deviation [SD]) for continuous variables and assessed the frequency (proportions) for categorical variables, utilizing weighted t-tests and chi-square tests accordingly. We utilized RCS analysis to visualize DI-GM-mortality linear association while adjusting for a multitude of potential covariates. The knot placement in the RCS curves was determined through the minimization of Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC).

Furthermore, we used Cox regression to estimate mortality risk ratios, reporting hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and tested the assumption of proportional hazards using Schoenfeld residuals. We adjusted for confounders in a three-model stepped approach: Model 1 remained unadjusted; Model 2 incorporated adjustments for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education level, marital status, and PIR levels; while Model 3 further adjusted preDM, history of CVD and cancer, energy intake, physical activity, ALT, AST, and alcohol consumption. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation techniques to maintain the integrity of the dataset.

Subgroup analyses, incorporating multiplicative interaction terms, were carried out to investigate whether the associations between the DI-GM and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality were modified by variables such as sex, age (< 40 or >= 40 years), race/ethnicity, education level, marital status, PIR levels, preDM, history of CVD, history of cancer, energy intake (< 2400 or >= 2400 kcal), and physical activity (< 200 or >= 200 METs-hour/week). To evaluate the robustness of our results, 6 sensitivity analyses were conducted. Sensitivity assessments were conducted exclusively based on model 3. Detail process was shown in the Supplementary Methods. All statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.1.2, and a two-tailed P value with a significance level of 0.05 was used for all statistical tests to determine significance.
Result
Baseline characteristics and comparative analyses

Supplementary Table S1 presents the baseline characteristics of the 13,390 participants enrolled in the study. Participants were categorized into two groups based on their survival status: Survivor group (n = 12,219) and non-Survivor group (n = 1171). It was found that, compared to the Survivor group, the non-Survivor group exhibited a lower DI-GM score (Survivors vs non-Survivors: 5.12 +- 0.03 vs 4.95 +- 0.07, p = 0.009). Additionally, a higher prevalence of MASLD was observed in the non-Survivor group (Survivors vs non-Survivors: 25.33% vs 31.82%, p = 0.001).

To further investigate the demographic characteristics of MASLD patients, participants were divided into two subgroups: MASLD (n = 3538, 26.4%) and non-MASLD (n = 9852, 73.6%). The results are presented in Table 1. It showed that compared to non-MASLD participants, MASLD patients were more likely to be male, non-Hispanic white, married, older, and have a lower educational level. They also more frequently had comorbidities such as cancer and CVD, a history of preDM, and engaged in less physical activity. Importantly, MASLD patients exhibited a lower DI-GM score (non-MASLD vs MASLD: 5.15 +- 0.03 vs 5.00 +- 0.04, p = 0.002) and had a higher mortality (non-MASLD vs MASLD: 5.66%vs 7.62%, p = 0.001). Among all causes of death, cardiovascular mortality was the most common, with a higher incidence in the MASLD group compared to the non-MASLD group (non-MALSD vs MASLD: 25.31%vs 33.74%, p < 0.001).

To delve deeper into the correlation between the DI-GM and all-cause/ cardiovascular mortality, we employed Restricted Cubic Spline (RCS) analysis to visually represent the relationship between DI-GM and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality (Fig. 2). The findings indicated a clear linear association between DI-GM and the risk of all-cause/cardiovascular mortality in both the non-MASLD and MASLD populations (non-linear P > 0.05). Additionally, we compared the fit of a linear model (DI-GM as a linear term) and an RCS model (DI-GM as a restricted cubic spline with 3 knots). The linear model had a lower AIC compared to the RCS model (All-cause mortality: Liner model = 20,978.36, RCS model = 20,974.82; Cardiovascular mortality: Liner model = 6088.961, RCS model = 6088.032), suggesting that the linear relationship is sufficient.

The adjusted analysis demonstrated that the global p-value of the Schoenfeld residuals exceeded 0.05, implying that the proportional hazards assumption was satisfied (Figure S1). The analyses revealed a significant inverse correlation between an increase in DI-GM and a decrease in the risk of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in both the presence and absence of MASLD. Notably, in Model 3, the reduction in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk was more pronounced among MASLD with higher DI-GM, compared to non-MASLD (all-cause mortality, HR = 0.87, 95% CI = 0.78 to 0.98, p = 0.02; cardiovascular mortality, HR = 0.805, 95% CI = 0.690 to 0.938, p = 0.005). To investigate the impact of the DI-GM on mortality within different subgroups of MASLD participants, we conducted subgroup analyses (Figs. 4, 5). The results indicated that age and preDM played significant roles in the relationship between DI-GM and mortality. To validate the robustness of our findings, we conducted 6 sensitivity analyses (Table 3). In all sensitivity analyses, the negative association between DI-GM and all-cause/cardiovascular mortality remained significant, demonstrating the robustness of our results.
Discussion

This study innovatively identified a significant inverse association between an elevated DI-GM and the risk of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, with particularly pronounced effects observed in participants with MASLD. Specifically, for every one-unit increase in DI-GM, there was a 13% reduction in the risk of all-cause mortality and a 19.5% reduction in the risk of cardiovascular mortality. Moreover, a more marked negative correlation between DI-GM and cardiovascular mortality was detected in MASLD with advanced fibrosis. Subgroup analyses revealed interactions between DI-GM and the risk of all-cause/cardiovascular mortality, including age and prDM status. Upon stratifying by age, a significant negative correlation between the DI-GM and all-cause mortality was observed solely within the MASLD patients aged below 40 years. In contrast, among patients over the age of 40, the negative correlation between the DI-GM and cardiovascular mortality was more pronounced. In terms of prDM status, a significant negative correlation between DI-GM and all-cause mortality was found only in participants (included preDM) without diabetes mellitus (DM), whereas a higher DI-GM score was associated with a significant reduction in cardiovascular mortality risk in those with prDM. Alternatively, six sensitivity analyses further validated the robustness of our findings.

MASLD is a well-established independent risk factor for mortality, with growing evidence highlighting CVD as a predominant concern in this population. Notably, MASLD patients face a substantially higher risk of CVD-related mortality compared to liver-related mortality. Consistent with this, our study revealed that the mortality rate among MASLD participants was significantly elevated compared to non-MASLD individuals (MASLD vs. non-MASLD: 7.62% vs. 5.66%, p = 0.001). Strikingly, cardiovascular mortality represented the leading cause of death in MASLD patients, accounting for 33.74% of all deaths. This phenomenon can be attributed to shared pathophysiological mechanisms, including insulin resistance (IR), endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress (OS), systemic inflammation, dysregulated lipoprotein metabolism, increased thrombogenicity, ectopic fat deposition, and gut microbiota dysbiosis. These interconnected pathways underscore the intricate relationship between MASLD and CVD, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. Given the profound impact of MASLD on cardiovascular health and overall mortality, there is an urgent imperative to identify and implement daily interventions capable of mitigating these risks.

Dietary indices serve as invaluable tools for characterizing dietary patterns based on dietary assessment data. Among these, the DI-GM, developed by Bezawit E. Kase and colleagues, represents a groundbreaking advancement. DI-GM uniquely captures the beneficial or detrimental effects of dietary components on gut microbiota, as evidenced by changes in microbial diversity indices, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and the abundance of specific bacterial species.

In this study, the correlation between DI-GM and indirect biomarkers of gut microbiota diversity provides compelling evidence of reduced microbial diversity in MASLD patients. Notably, our findings reveal that DI-GM were significantly lower in MASLD patients compared to non-MASLD individuals, suggesting that MASLD patients exhibit a diminished capacity to maintain a healthy gut microbiome through their regular dietary intake. This observation aligns with a robust body of prior research highlighting systemic pathological alterations in the gut microbiota of MASLD patients.For instance, a recent systematic review demonstrated that MASLD patients exhibit reduced alpha diversity, decreased populations of beneficial genera such as Coprococcus, Faecalibacterium, and Ruminococcus genera,, and an overgrowth of Escherichia compared to healthy controls.

Furthermore, a distinct microbial signature, particularly the prominence of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, has been identified as uniquely associated with MASLD in human studies. Mechanistically, the bidirectional communication between the gut microbiota and the liver, termed the "gut-liver axis" (GLA), plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis and progression of MASLD. Collectively, these studies, along with our findings, underscore the critical role of gut microbiota in the mortality process of MASLD patients.

Dietary nutrients exert profound effects on MASLD by modulating gut microbiota diversity, altering the Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio, and promoting the growth of beneficial microbial species. Fiber, a key beneficial dietary component included in DI-GM, has been shown to enhance gut microbes that metabolize choline, thereby reducing its bioavailability and generating metabolites such as trimethylamine. Conversely, a fiber-deficient diet leads to mucin-degrading bacteria overgrowth, compromising mucosal thickness. DI-GM further distinguishes itself from other dietary indices by incorporating fermented dairy products as a unique component. These products, including yogurt, cheese, and kefir, are rich in lactobacilli and lactic acid, which have been scientifically validated to increase the abundance of Lactobacillus species within the gut microbiota. Recent evidence highlights that fermented dairy products, particularly yogurt, are more effective than non-fermented dairy in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic risk biomarkers. On the other hand, high-fat diets, recognized as detrimental dietary components in DI-GM, disrupt the gut microbiome, impair intestinal and vascular barriers, promote bacterial translocation, and exacerbate systemic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation. The liver, being highly exposed to portal systemic products, is particularly vulnerable to these effects. High-fat diets are also associated with elevated levels of lipopolysaccharides (LPS), a known risk factor for MASLD. Consistent with these findings, our study demonstrates that improving DI-GM scores in MASLD patients is associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality. These results underscore the critical importance of dietary interventions that target gut microbiota modulation as a strategy to enhance survival outcomes in MASLD patients.

This study further revealed that higher DI-GM scores in MASLD patients are associated with lower cardiovascular mortality. Mechanistically, gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in this process by converting dietary choline and L-carnitine into trimethylamine (TMA), which is subsequently oxidized in the liver to form trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO). TMAO has been implicated in endothelial dysfunction and is strongly associated with cardiovascular risks such as atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction. Additionally, systemic inflammation triggered by gut dysbiosis and the translocation of microbial products exacerbates endothelial dysfunction and accelerates atherosclerosis, both of which are central to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Furthermore, microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and bile acids, influence blood pressure regulation and vascular health, further underscoring the gut microbiota's role in cardiovascular outcomes. These findings, combined with our research, highlight the critical importance of a gut microbiota-healthy diet, as quantified by DI-GM, in mitigating cardiovascular mortality among MASLD patients. By modulating gut microbiota composition and function, dietary interventions can address the underlying mechanisms linking gut dysbiosis to cardiovascular risks, offering a promising avenue for improving clinical outcomes.

Dysbiosis of the gut microbiota in MASLD is a key driver of increased liver fibrosis, and as liver disease progresses to advanced stages, the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) becomes significantly elevated. Our findings underscore this relationship, revealing a particularly strong association between the DI-GM and mortality in MASLD patients with advanced fibrosis, especially those at high risk of cardiovascular events. This suggests that the interplay between gut microbiota dysbiosis, liver fibrosis, and cardiovascular health is a critical axis in the pathophysiology of MASLD. In light of these insights, we propose that dietary interventions aimed at enhancing gut microbiota health should be prioritized for MASLD patients with advanced fibrosis and elevated cardiovascular risk. Such targeted dietary modifications, guided by the DI-GM, have the potential to significantly improve cardiovascular outcomes. By addressing the gut-liver-heart axis, this approach offers a holistic strategy to reduce mortality in this high-risk population.

The global prevalence of MASLD is on a concerning upward trajectory, with the most pronounced increase observed among individuals under the age of 40. Our subgroup analyses revealed that younger MASLD patients (under 40 years) can more effectively reduce their risk of all-cause mortality by improving their DI-GM through targeted dietary modifications, thereby promoting gut microbiota stability. In contrast, for patients over 40, an elevated DI-GM was more strongly associated with a reduction in cardiovascular mortality risk. From a mechanistic perspective, the regenerative capacity of liver cells in younger individuals is relatively stronger. Higher DI-GM score may exert hepatoprotective effects by modulating gut microbiota composition, thereby creating a more favorable microenvironment for liver function. This could promote hepatic cell repair and regeneration. For instance, metabolites produced by certain beneficial bacteria may stimulate hepatic cell proliferation, alleviate steatosis and fibrosis, and reduce the risk of complications arising from progressive liver disease, ultimately lowering all-cause mortality. Furthermore, the immune system in younger populations is more active and sensitive. Higher DI-GM scores may enhance the interaction between gut microbiota and the immune system, activating beneficial immune components such as T and B cells. This could enhance the secretion of anti-inflammatory cytokines by immune cells, thereby reducing all-cause mortality. However, with aging, the elasticity and function of vascular walls progressively decline. Higher DI-GM scores may confer vascular protective effects by modulating gut microbiota to produce beneficial metabolites, such as SCFAs. These SCFAs can act on vascular endothelial cells, enhancing endothelial function, increasing vascular elasticity, and reducing vascular resistance. Improved vascular function may mitigate the risk of cardiovascular diseases, thereby lowering cardiovascular mortality. Moreover, older individuals often exhibit dyslipidemia and chronic low-grade inflammation, which are critical risk factors for cardiovascular diseases. Higher DI-GM scores may alleviate these risks by regulating gut microbiota to modulate lipid absorption and metabolism, while simultaneously suppressing the activation of inflammatory signaling pathways. This age-dependent association underscores the importance of tailoring dietary strategies to the unique physiological and microbial profiles of different age groups. For younger patients, interventions focused on enhancing gut microbiota diversity and stability may offer a proactive approach to mitigating long-term health risks. For older patients, dietary modifications that specifically target cardiovascular risk factors through gut microbiota modulation could provide significant clinical benefits. These insights not only emphasize the critical role of the gut-liver axis in MASLD progression but also pave the way for personalized, age-stratified nutritional strategies to improve outcomes across the lifespan.

Subgroup analyses further illuminated that the prediabetes (preDM) status of patients significantly modulates the efficacy of the DI-GM in reducing mortality risk. Specifically, while DI-GM was more effective in lowering overall mortality risk in non-diabetic patients, elevating the DI-GM in prediabetic patients demonstrated a stronger association with reducing cardiovascular mortality. This differential effect underscores the complex interplay between metabolic health and gut microbiota in shaping clinical outcomes. This may be attributed to the synergistic interplay between DI-GM and metabolic pathways. Prediabetes is associated with a heightened cardiovascular risk. A high DI-GM score may confer protective effects by enhancing gut barrier integrity through mechanisms involving short-chain fatty acids, prebiotics, and dietary fiber etc. Furthermore, it may mitigate cardiovascular mortality risk through multiple pathways, including improved insulin sensitivity, reduced oxidative stress, regulated immune responses, and modulation of choline-metabolizing bacteria to suppress trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) production.

In the context of cardiovascular mortality, insulin resistance is a central driver. It impairs glucose output and fatty acid metabolism, leading to elevated triglyceride levels and increased secretion of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) by the liver. These metabolic disturbances are compounded by endothelial dysfunction, characterized by reduced nitric oxide production and increased release of procoagulant factors, which promote platelet aggregation and vascular inflammation. Collectively, these mechanisms contribute to the development of atherosclerotic plaques and elevate the risk of cardiovascular mortality. These findings highlight the potential of DI-GM as a tool for personalized dietary strategies tailored to the metabolic status of MASLD patients. Notably, individuals without diabetes, including those with prediabetes (preDM), appear to derive greater mortality reduction benefits from such dietary improvements. This suggests that early intervention, particularly in prediabetic patients, could disrupt the progression of metabolic dysfunction and its downstream consequences.

Given the pivotal role of the gut microbiota in various diseases, DI-GM can be utilized to investigate diet-disease associations similar to those of established indices such as Alternate Healthy Eating Index (AHEI) and Alternate Mediterranean Diet (aMED) et al. However, a key distinction of DI-GM lies in its inclusion of specific foods rather than broad food groups for certain components. During the development of DI-GM, most review articles primarily focused on dietary intervention studies targeting specific foods. Incorporating specific foods into DI-GM may offer potential benefits in refining dietary recommendations. Additionally, the aMED emphasizes the consumption of olive oil, whole grains, vegetables, and fish, but its core assumption:that "food itself directly determines health outcomes":fails to account for individual variations in gut microbiota-mediated metabolism of dietary components. In contrast, DI-GM quantifies the regulatory effects of dietary patterns on gut microbiota, thereby more accurately reflecting the impact of diet on metabolic health (e.g., MASLD). Recent studies have highlighted the association between higher aMED, Dietary Approach to Stop Hypertension (DASH), and AHEI scores and reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in MASLD patients. A cross-sectional study further demonstrated a linear inverse relationship between dietary quality and all-cause mortality in MASLD patients, suggesting that improved dietary quality may enhance survival outcomes. However, contradictory evidence also exists: Yoo et al. found that while higher dietary quality was linked to reduced all-cause mortality in individuals without MASLD, no such association was observed in MASLD patients. These findings underscore the importance of dietary quality as a modifiable factor in MASLD management. Notably, this study did not further explore the comparative effectiveness of DI-GM against established indices (e.g., aMED, DASH) in predicting MASLD outcomes. Future research should integrate DI-GM with traditional dietary indices through multivariable models to evaluate their independent predictive value for MASLD-related endpoints.

A notable strength of our study including the analysis of a nationally representative sample of diverse populations in the United States, and the inclusion of a large number of potential confounding factors in the availability of data on analysis and long-term mortality. These strengths enhance the generalizability of the findings to the general population. Secondly, To the best of our knowledge, this is the first investigation to examine the relationship between the DI-GM and mortality risk in both MASLD and non-MASLD populations, we have found that MASLD patients can reduce their mortality risk by improving their daily diet, a finding that was confirmed to be robust through six sensitivity analyses. Lastly, in comparison with other dietary indices, DI-GM encompasses a broader spectrum of targets, incorporating measures such as diversity indices, the production of short-chain fatty acids, variations in phyla, and the outcomes of specific bacterial species. This comprehensive approach allows for a more nuanced understanding of the dietary influences on gut microbiota composition and function. The scoring system of DI-GM is straightforward and user-friendly, making it highly suitable for widespread adoption in both clinical and public health settings. By quantifying the impact of dietary patterns on gut microbiota, DI-GM offers actionable and specific dietary recommendations for MASLD patients, demonstrating significant practical value in guiding personalized nutrition strategies. This ease of application, combined with its scientific rigor, positions DI-GM as a valuable tool for improving patient outcomes and advancing dietary interventions in metabolic health management.

Despite these strengths, our study has several limitations. Firstly, the NHANES data, which are based on self-reported information from individuals, may be prone to recall bias. Self-reported dietary data, while commonly used in large-scale cohort studies, are subject to limitations such as recall bias, social desirability bias, and underreporting, particularly for complex dietary patterns. These factors could introduce measurement error into DI-GM scores, potentially affecting the observed associations with MASLD and mortality. To mitigate these biases, we utilized standardized dietary assessment tools:24-h dietary recalls. However, we recognize that these limitations may still impact the precision of DI-GM as a dietary biomarker. Secondly, the cross-sectional design of NHANES precludes the provision of insights into the temporal changes of these variables, which limits the further exploration of the dynamics of the DI-GM. Thirdly, the use of non-invasive FLI, NFS, APRI, and FIB4 scores as diagnostic criteria for steatosis and advanced liver fibrosis may introduce inaccuracies in estimating the true risk extent of MASLD and advanced liver fibrosis, although these scores have been validated as reliable diagnostic tools in the U.S. population. Fourthly, the relatively small number of cancer-related deaths in the MASLD patient population led us to exclude cancer-related mortality from our focus. Therefore, well-designed prospective longitudinal studies are warranted to further investigate the impact of the DI-GM on all-cause mortality risk in patients with MASLD. Lastly, In the subgroup analysis of this study, the limited sample sizes in certain specific subgroups may restrict the generalizability of the findings, and further in-depth analyses of these subgroups are warranted. Meanwhile, future studies should validate our findings using histological confirmation of MASLD and fibrosis, particularly in populations with high variability in diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, advanced imaging techniques (e.g., MRI-based proton density fat fraction) could reduce misclassification bias.
Conclusion

In this study, the DI-GM has filled a critical research gap by revealing a significant inverse correlation between DI-GM scores and both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients with MASLD. This groundbreaking finding not only validates the scientific value of DI-GM but also provides robust evidence to support dietary interventions aimed at improving outcomes in MASLD patients. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that the mortality-reducing effects of DI-GM are particularly pronounced in MASLD patients with advanced fibrosis and are influenced by age and prediabetes status. These insights highlight the potential of DI-GM to offer personalized dietary recommendations tailored to specific patient subgroups, thereby advancing the application of precision medicine in MASLD management. The application of DI-GM opens new avenues for future research, such as exploring its relationship with other metabolic diseases (e.g., diabetes, obesity) or using multi-omics technologies to further elucidate the mechanisms underlying diet-microbiota-host interactions.

BACKGROUND: Fabry disease (FD) is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-Gal A (alpha-galactosidase A) deficiency, resulting in multiorgan accumulation of sphingolipid, namely globotriaosylceramide. This triggers ventricular myocardial hypertrophy, fibrosis, and inflammation, driving arrhythmia and sudden death. Atrial fibrillation is common, yet the cellular mechanisms accounting for this are unknown. METHODS: To address this, we conducted ECG analysis from a large cohort of 115 adults with FD at varying cardiomyopathy stages. ECG P-wave characteristics were compared with non-FD controls. Cellular contractile and electrophysiological function were examined in a novel atrial cellular FD model developed and imputed into in silico atrial models to provide insight into mechanisms of arrhythmia. Induced pluripotent stem cells were genome-edited using Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats-Cas9 to introduce the GLA p.N215S variant and differentiated into induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs). Contraction, calcium handling, and electrophysiology experiments were conducted. Bi-atrial in silico models were developed with cellular changes as in GLA p.N215S iPSC-CMs. RESULTS: ECG analysis demonstrated P-wave duration and PQ interval shortening in FD adults before the onset of cardiomyopathy. Patients with FD exhibited a higher incidence of premature atrial contractions and increased risk of atrial fibrillation compared with healthy controls. GLA p.N215S iPSC-CMs were deficient in alpha-Gal A and exhibited globotriaosylceramide accumulation. Atrial GLA p.N215S iPSC-CMs demonstrated a more positive diastolic membrane potential, faster action potential upstroke velocity, greater incidence of delayed afterdepolarizations, greater contraction force, and alterations in calcium handling compared with wild-type iPSC-CMs. Simulations with these changes in the in silico models resulted in similar P-wave morphology changes to those seen in early FD cardiomyopathy and increased atrial fibrillation vulnerability. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide novel insights into underpinning mechanisms for atrial arrhythmia and a rationale for early P-wave changes in FD. These may be targeted to develop therapeutic strategies to reduce the arrhythmic burden in FD.

passages.text: Prescription Patterns in Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK): A European Survey.

PURPOSE: To assess current prescription patterns in Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK) in Europe. SETTING: Countries affiliated with the European Cornea and Cell Transplantation Registry (ECCTR) and the European Vision Institute Clinical Research Network (EVICR.net). DESIGN: Cross-sectional study (European survey). METHODS: An electronic survey was distributed to 16 national societies to gather data on prescription patterns for DMEK. Responses were categorized by three clinical goals: prevention of postoperative endophthalmitis, graft rejection, and pupillary block and glaucoma. RESULTS: Responses from 136 surgeons revealed that medication protocols mainly came from departmental protocols (54%) or personal experiences (48%) rather than national guidelines (22%) (multiple answers were allowed). Infection prevention primarily relied on intraoperative (72%) and postoperative (92%) antibiotics, with preoperative use less common (18%). Steroids were the mainstay for rejection prevention, used intraoperatively (59%), postoperatively (100%), and occasionally preoperatively (13%). Steroids were typically tapered to once daily after six months (46%) and discontinued after varying durations (65%). Dexamethasone was the preferred steroid. For high-risk DMEK, the most common approach was adding another topical (30%) or systemic immunosuppressive drug (24%), such as cyclosporine or mycophenolate. For graft rejection, most respondents increased topical steroid frequency (85%) or added (peri)bulbar steroid injections (42%). Pupillary block and glaucoma prophylaxis mainly involved intraoperative mydriatics (34%); intraocular pressure-lowering agents were rarely used (0.7-2.2%). For steroid-induced ocular hypertension, the common approach was switching to a lower-potency steroid (40%) or reducing steroid frequency (43%). CONCLUSIONS: Current prescription patterns in routine and high-risk DMEK vary significantly, reflecting the lack of standardized guidelines.
